sections.title: Human language and computation
Speech movements in MRI

teaching.text: **Real-time MRI films the inside of the head while a person talks**, so the hidden movements of speech can be watched directly. The view is a side view cut down the middle of the head, with the face pointing left. Air appears black, and soft tissue such as the tongue, lips and throat walls appears gray and white.
children: The **lips** sit at the far left. The **tongue** is the large rounded mass filling most of the mouth, and it is the most active structure in speech.

The roof of the mouth has a bony front part, the **hard palate**, and a soft movable back part, the **soft palate** or **velum**, which lifts to seal off the nose or lowers to let air out through the nose.
Behind the tongue, the **pharynx** runs down the throat to the **larynx**, which holds the **vocal folds**.

teaching.text: **During speech all of these structures move at the same time and at high speed.** Each sound depends on a precise shape of the whole passage, and the shapes flow smoothly into one another. The two movies differ almost entirely in where the tongue and lips are placed.

sections.title: Why speech is a remarkable learned skill

teaching.text: **We learn to move our speech organs in extremely complex ways with no instructions and almost no visual feedback.** A child cannot see their own tongue, soft palate or vocal folds, yet **by ages 2 to 4** children speak with a wide vocabulary and near-adult language.
children: **Reading and writing** whole words usually comes at **ages 6 to 7** and requires a great deal of instruction, even though the eyes and hands are fully visible. Speech is a deep human cognitive skill that the brain is prepared to acquire.

teaching.text: **Articulatory phonetics** studies the movements of the different structures of the **vocal tract**, the full air passage from the larynx to the lips with a side branch into the nose. Real-time MRI is one of its main tools.

**In the last two years, voice assistants and other speech technology have come to emulate human speech ability.** To **emulate** an ability means to reproduce its behavior. **LING 285 is about both human speech and AI speech**, so the human skill and the machine version can be compared directly.

sections.title: Air vibration and acoustic phonetics

teaching.text: **Focus on the air between the tongue and the rest of the vocal tract.** Ignoring the curve of the real tract turns it into a simple **tube of air**, open at the **lips** and treated as closed at the **larynx**.
children: The tube is labeled **schwa**, the neutral relaxed vowel. For schwa the tongue does not narrow the passage much anywhere, so the air space is about the same width from end to end, and the straight even tube fits it best.

teaching.text: **The air inside the tube vibrates by shifting back and forth, not by flowing out the end.** Each column of air shifts around its own resting position.
children: Where neighboring columns move toward each other, the air is packed tightly into a **compression**. Where they move apart, the air spreads out into a **rarefaction**.
These regions travel along the tube and reflect back from its ends. This repeating pattern is the **vibration of air** that makes up the sound of the vowel.

teaching.text: **Acoustic phonetics** studies how air vibrates in the vocal tract and what sound results. Articulatory phonetics describes the shape of the tube, and acoustic phonetics describes the air inside it. Moving the tongue and lips changes the tube, and changing the tube changes how the air vibrates.

sections.title: Why scientific understanding of AI matters

teaching.text: **AI brings real psychological, economic, social and environmental harms, and many scientists warn about existential harm.** Pretending it does not exist is not a workable option, because it exists, with many harms and some benefits such as **immunotherapy** and **environmental engineering**.
children: The environmental case cuts both ways. Running large AI systems uses enormous energy, while AI tools are also applied to problems that could help the environment.

teaching.text: **One of the biggest dangers is that we have no idea how AI works.** We know everything, because every number inside a system can be inspected, and understand nothing, because no one can explain why it gives the answers it does.
children: The people who know how these systems operate are very few, which puts decisions about AI in very few hands.

teaching.text: **AI literacy is necessary** for scientists who use AI, politicians who need to control it, and lawyers who litigate cases involving it. A creative thinker in a class like this one can help us understand these systems well enough to benefit from them while avoiding their negative consequences.

sections.title: Course goals

teaching.text: **The course has four specific goals.** To appreciate the human cognitive skill of **speech**. To understand basic principles of **physics** through speech. To understand how modern **AI systems model human cognition**. To sharpen **methodical reasoning** through **elementary programming**, which forces each step of a problem to be stated clearly and in order.

**The course also has three general goals.** To think creatively in a rich **interdisciplinary** way across physics, psychology, linguistics, biology, economics, computer science, philosophy and neuroscience. To deepen understanding of the world we live in today. To sharpen the **skillful use of modern AI systems**.

sections.title: Moving from memorization to creative reasoning

teaching.text: **Diotima's ladder describes the climb from surface knowledge of particular things toward deep understanding of the general ideas behind them.** Diotima, around 440 BCE, taught **Socrates**, who taught **Plato**, who taught **Aristotle**.

**The bottom of the ladder holds daily experience, habit, memorization, specialized skills, repetition, replication and textbooks.** Its rule is that **similar is same, and slight difference is different**.

**The top of the ladder holds creativity, insight, thought, focus, attention, imagination, vision, problem-posing, problem-solving, critical reading and creative writing.** Its rule is the reverse of the first one. **Different can be same, and similar can be different.**
children: The sounds f and v sound different, yet they are made in the same place in the mouth. The two th sounds are spelled the same, yet one is voiced and the other is not.
**Problem-posing** means asking good questions in the first place. **Problem-solving** means answering questions once they have been asked.

teaching.text: **A person climbs the ladder through repeated cycles of question and answer**, the method Socrates became famous for.
**For about 2500 years, people could fake it** by memorizing, repeating and replicating. In 2026, interviews for jobs and graduate school look for the properties at the top of the ladder.

sections.title: Voicing and place through sustained fricatives

teaching.text: **Produce the sounds and notice what the body does.** Hold the **f** in "fat" and switch to the **v** in "vat." Hold the **th** in "thing" and switch to the **th** in "that." Hold **s** and switch to **z**. Hold the **sh** in "mesh" and switch to the buzzing sound in the middle of "beige," written **j** here.

**Within each pair, the difference is voice, which is whether the vocal folds vibrate.** With fingers on the throat, f, the first th, s and sh feel still and hiss, while v, the second th, z and the sound in "beige" buzz.
children: The **vocal folds** are two small folds of tissue inside the larynx. Held apart, they let air pass silently and the sound is **voiceless**. Brought close together, they vibrate in the airflow and the sound is **voiced**. The tongue and lips do not change within a pair.

teaching.text: **From one line to the next, the difference is place of articulation, where the narrowing is formed.** The lower lip at the upper teeth for f and v, the tongue tip at the upper teeth for th, the tongue tip near the ridge behind the teeth for s and z, and the tongue a bit further back for sh and the sound in "beige."
**Voice and place of articulation are two separate, independent properties of a speech sound.**

sections.title: The fricative system

teaching.text: **All of these sounds are fricatives**, made by bringing two parts of the vocal tract very close together without closing the passage. Air forced through the narrow gap becomes turbulent, which produces the hissing or buzzing noise, and the sound can be held as long as there is breath.

**The fricative table has voice in the rows and place of articulation in the columns.** The places are **labial** (the lower lip at the upper teeth, for f and v), **dental** (the tongue tip at the teeth, for the two th sounds), **alveolar** (the tongue tip near the **alveolar ridge** just behind the upper teeth, for s and z) and **postalveolar** (the front of the tongue a little further back, for sh and the sound in "beige").

**Two fricatives in the same column differ only in voicing, and two in the same row differ only in place.** English spells the two th sounds the same way even though one is voiceless and the other is voiced.

sections.title: Stop place, voicing, and nasality

teaching.text: **Stops close the passage completely for a brief moment.** Pressure builds up behind the closure, and the release lets the trapped air burst out, which makes a stop short and sharp. A stop cannot be held as a continuous sound.

**The English stops form a grid of three places and three types.** The first row, **p, b and m**, closes the **lips**. The second row, **t, d and n**, presses the tongue tip against the **alveolar ridge**. The third row, **k, g and ng**, raises the **back of the tongue** against the **soft palate**.
children: Across each row, the place stays the same. The first sound is **voiceless**, the second is **voiced**, and the third is a **nasal**, which is voiced with the **soft palate lowered** so air flows out through the nose.

teaching.text: **The columns follow the fricative table's logic.** The voiceless stops are **p, t and k**, the voiced stops are **b, d and g**, and the nasal stops are **m, n and ng**. Three places of closure combined with three settings of the vocal folds and soft palate give nine sounds.

lecture02.title: 02 · Speech structure and learning in AI

sections.title: Human language and technology
Lecture agenda
Internal coordination during speech

teaching.text: **Real-time MRI films the inside of the head while a person is talking.** The images are **midsagittal**, a side-view slice down the middle of the head, with the face pointing left. **Air shows up black** and soft tissue shows up gray or white, so the dark spaces are the open airways, the mouth, the nasal passages and the **pharynx** behind the tongue.
children: The **tongue** is the large gray mass filling the mouth. Above it is the bony **hard palate**, and hanging from its back is the **velum**, or soft palate, which closes or opens the path from the throat into the nose.

teaching.text: **The tongue, lips, jaw and velum all move at once and very quickly.** Every consonant and vowel is the result of shaping this tube of air in a particular way. **Phonetics** is the study of these speech sounds.

sections.title: Fricative place and voicing

teaching.text: **A fricative is made by bringing two parts of the mouth very close together without closing them completely.** Air pushed through the narrow gap becomes turbulent, which makes the hissing or buzzing noise, and the sound can be held as long as there is breath.

**Fricatives are organized by place of articulation, where the gap is formed, and by voicing, whether the vocal folds vibrate.** A **voiceless** sound has only the hiss. A **voiced** sound adds a buzz that can be felt with a hand on the throat during "zzzz" but not "ssss."
children: **Labial** f and v raise the lower lip against the upper teeth. **Dental** th in "think" and th in "this" put the tongue tip at the upper teeth. **Alveolar** s and z raise the tongue tip toward the **alveolar ridge** behind the upper teeth. **Postalveolar** sh and j, the sound in "measure," form the gap a little farther back.

teaching.text: **Each pair is made with the same place and the same manner.** The only difference between f and v, or s and z, is whether the vocal folds vibrate. The four MRI images show the constriction moving backward from the lips to behind the ridge.

sections.title: Oral and nasal stop comparisons

teaching.text: **A stop closes the vocal tract completely, so air cannot get out through the mouth.** Pressure builds behind the closure and bursts out when it is released. English has **oral stops** and **nasal stops**.
children: In an **oral stop**, or **plosive**, the velum is raised to seal off the nose, so pressure builds and is released as a burst. In a **nasal stop**, the mouth is closed the same way but the velum is lowered, so air flows out through the nose the whole time and the sound hums.

teaching.text: **Each of three places has a voiceless oral stop, a voiced oral stop and a nasal stop.** At the **lips**, p, b and m. At the **alveolar ridge**, t, d and n. At the **velum**, k, g and ng, the sound at the end of "sing," which are called **velar**.
children: In the MRI images, m, n and ng have the velum hanging down away from the back of the throat, while p, t and k have it raised. A stop is an event in time. First the closure, then pressure or nasal airflow, then the release.

sections.title: Three dimensions of consonant knowledge

teaching.text: **The fricatives and stops fit into one table built on manner of articulation, place of articulation and voice.** Manner is how the air is shaped, a narrow gap, a closure with the nose sealed, or a closure with the nose open. The places run from front to back, **labial, dental, alveolar, postalveolar** and **velar**.

**Every consonant is a combination of three values.** The sound t is a **voiceless alveolar oral stop**, and z is a **voiced alveolar fricative**. Changing one value gives a different sound, so t becomes d by adding voice, and d becomes n by opening the nose.

**The empty cells matter too.** English has no dental or postalveolar stops and no velar fricative. The sounds of English form a **highly structured system**, and every speaker uses it without ever having been taught the table.

sections.title: AI as a model of psychological abilities

teaching.text: **Artificial intelligence is a model of five psychological skills that animals have, knowing, recognizing, attending, acting and learning.** Knowing is stored usable information, recognizing is identifying what arrives, attending is selecting what to focus on, acting is producing an output, and learning is changing with experience.
**How AI models each skill is at least slightly based on how humans do it.** AI is not a technical innovation that came out of nowhere. It grew out of ideas about human and animal psychology.

sections.title: Taylor’s cloze procedure

teaching.text: **How AI knows something connects to Wilson L. Taylor's 1953 paper "Cloze Procedure," subtitled A New Tool for Measuring Readability**, published in the Fall 1953 issue of **Journalism Quarterly**. It reported three pilot studies and two experiments comparing cloze results with two **readability formulas**.

**Taylor asked whether people's ability to restore deleted parts of a message could measure how readable that message was.** A tool built to measure human understanding of language ended up describing what it means for a system to know something.

sections.title: Closure turns incomplete input into a whole pattern

teaching.text: **Taylor called cloze procedure a new psychological tool for measuring the effectiveness of communication.** The method is straightforward, the data are easily counted, and its results agreed with the **Flesch** and **Dale-Chall** readability formulas. He credited the experimental psychologists **Charles Osgood** and **Melvin Marks** for starting the work.

**A cloze is the unit of measurement, pronounced like "close," and named after closure.** **Closure** is the Gestalt psychology term for the human tendency to **complete a familiar pattern that is not quite finished**, such as seeing a broken circle as whole.
children: The three black circles with wedges cut out produce a bright white triangle that is not actually drawn. The visual system completes the triangle from the partial information.

sections.title: What successful completion requires

teaching.text: **The same principle applies to language.** Given "Chickens cackle and ___ quack," almost anyone supplies "ducks." Supplying the removed word scores **one cloze unit**.
children: Filling that blank takes the **meanings** and **forms** of all five words, the meanings of their **combinations**, and the parallel structure that pairs an animal with its sound.

teaching.text: **Taylor defined a cloze unit as a successful attempt to reproduce a part deleted from a message by deciding from the remaining context what is missing.** **Cloze procedure** intercepts a message from a transmitter, deletes parts, and gives the damaged message to receivers, whose repairs produce countable cloze units.

**AI shows its knowledge of something by completing, or clozing, sequences.** A teacher tests a student the same way, by asking for the rest of a sequence. From the AI point of view, **knowledge is nothing more than completion**.

sections.title: From words to vectors and next-word probabilities

teaching.text: **GPT takes in a sequence of words and predicts the next one.** To a computer, a word is **a bunch of random numbers**, with the one requirement that **no two words share the same numbers**. Such a list is a **vector**, and one word's vector could hold 1024 numbers, drawn as a tall bar for each of "chickens," "cackle," "and" and "ducks."

**For "chickens cackle and ducks ___," a system that knows English outputs a vector of 10,000 numbers, each the probability that a given English word comes next.** "Quack" gets a high probability, while "cat" and "Zulu" get very low ones. Its knowledge of English shows up entirely in how well it completes the blank.

sections.title: Weights carry the system’s learned knowledge

teaching.text: **The list of probabilities is called a pdf, a probability distribution function, and the input vectors are the x's.** GPT turns the x's into the pdf by **recognizing by computing**, and the computing is mostly **addition, subtraction, multiplication and division**, grade school arithmetic done an enormous number of times.

**The knowledge that transforms the x's into the pdf is stored in numbers called w's, or weights.** The x's change with every sentence, the w's stay fixed while the system is used, and changing the weights changes the knowledge. Today's systems have **about a couple of trillion weights**.

sections.title: Weights and synapses as a scale comparison

teaching.text: **Trillions of weights are not too many to resemble human knowledge.** Knowing that chickens cackle but ducks quack is stored in the **synapses**, the connections between the **neurons** of the brain.

**The brain has about 150 trillion synapses, roughly 75 times the 2 trillion weights of today's AI systems.** In both cases knowledge is stored in a huge number of connection strengths rather than in a list of facts.

sections.title: Completion is a form of prediction

teaching.text: **Many people find "knowledge is completion" nonsensical, including Yann LeCun, who raised a billion dollars on that position.** Anyone who uses an AI system can judge for themselves whether its notion of knowledge is **totally different** from their own. One reasonable answer is that it is **not totally different**.

**Another term for completion is prediction, and that word sits better with people.** Humans constantly **predict** and **expect** what comes next, so knowledge as completion is knowledge as prediction.

sections.title: Mistakes provide a direction for learning

teaching.text: **AI learns by making mistakes, and humans may not be that different.** In the Reddit cartoon "How much you learn," the stack of books "From mistakes" is far taller than "From theory" or "From practice."
**The main learning algorithm in AI is Stochastic Gradient Descent, or SGD**, which can be understood through the very easy example of **averaging**.

sections.title: Averaging as observation-based error learning

teaching.text: **The ordinary way to average 10, 12 and 14 is to add them and divide by three, which gives 12.** This direct method does not work for speech, language, biological molecules or scenes, where no formula gives the answer in one step.

**The AI way starts with a wild guess x, then improves x by exposure to the data.** Take one number from the list, compare it with x, move x a bit closer to it, and repeat with another number. This is **observation-based error learning**.

sections.title: The correction rule of stochastic gradient descent

teaching.text: **SGD finds the average, the essence, of [78, 67, 98, 85, 76, 68, 98, 72] in five steps.** The true average is 80.25, but SGD never does that calculation.
children: Pick any random number as the estimate, so x[0] is 130. Randomly pick a data point, so d[0] is 98. Measure the mistake, the **Loss**, which is 130 minus 98, or 32. Subtract a small part of the Loss, 10 percent, so x[1] is 130 minus 3.2, which is 126.8. Repeat with another data point to get x[2], then x[3].

teaching.text: **If the estimate starts too low, the Loss is negative and subtracting it raises the estimate.** From 10 with a draw of 78, the estimate rises by 6.8 to 16.8. The estimate is always pushed toward the data.
**Stochastic means random, gradient refers to the Loss, and descent means reducing.** The algorithm makes an initial guess and uses data to improve it.

sections.title: Learning rate changes both speed and variability

teaching.text: **The fraction of the Loss subtracted at each step is the learning rate.** The four graphs plot the estimate x against 300 **epochs** for learning rates of 10, 50, 1 and 80 percent, each with runs starting from **initial conditions** of 130 (red), 80 (green) and 10 (blue).
children: At 10 percent, the red and blue runs reach the neighborhood of 80 within about 25 to 50 epochs and then wobble slightly. At 1 percent, the runs are smooth but very slow, still short of 80 after 300 epochs. At 50 percent, they arrive within a few epochs but then bounce between about 70 and 95. At 80 percent, the bouncing spreads from about 65 to 97.

teaching.text: **The bouncing comes from the random single data points.** A large learning rate moves the estimate most of the way toward whichever number was drawn, so a draw of 98 from an estimate of 80 at 80 percent jumps the estimate to 94.4, and the next draw may throw it far back down.

sections.title: The speed–accuracy tradeoff

teaching.text: **This is the fundamental learning tradeoff, written with the learning rate γ (gamma).** Raising γ raises speed and lowers accuracy, because the estimate arrives fast but keeps jumping. Lowering γ lowers speed and raises accuracy, because the estimate creeps but settles close to the true value.
**For generations, thousands of people have made their living by finding better ways to optimize learning**, so that speed and accuracy both increase at once.

sections.title: Dynamical systems 1
Lecture agenda
Elements, relations, and a goal

teaching.text: **A dynamical system is a system whose state changes over time according to rules.** This course meets them in **animal behavior**, such as an octopus defending its home or a person speaking, and in **AI learning**, where a program changes its internal numbers as it is trained.

**Every dynamical system has three parts, elements, relations and a goal.** The **elements** are the pieces, the **relations** are how the pieces are connected and coordinated, and the **goal** is what the whole system works to achieve. The same three parts describe an animal's body, a vocal tract or a learning program.

sections.title: An octopus coordinates its body with its environment

teaching.text: **An octopus defending its den is a dynamical system.** Its **elements** are its eight **arms** and the **ground**. Its **relations** are the coordinated connections between each arm, the ground and the fish, **planned by a neural system** in the octopus's head and throughout its body. Its **goal** is to **keep the den**.

sections.title: Speech is an organized dynamical system

teaching.text: **Human speech is a dynamical system with many more elements.** The **elements** are the **many parts of the tongue**, the **lips**, the **velum**, the **larynx**, the **palate** and the **pharyngeal wall**. The tongue counts as many parts because its tip, body and root move somewhat independently.

**The relations between all these parts are planned by the brain, and the goal is to convey a thought.** Producing a single word requires the lips, tongue, velum and larynx to move at precisely coordinated times. The MRI recording shows these parts moving together continuously over about three seconds of speech.

sections.title: Shared organization across very different systems

teaching.text: **All daily voluntary actions and the involuntary actions of the heart, pancreas and neurons are dynamical systems.** Their elements range from **organs** down to **cells** and the **chemicals** inside cells, so **biology, chemistry and physics** all study dynamical systems. The **speech system** is a **very complex** one.

**Because there are so many dynamical systems, one can be used to study another.** An octopus arm and a human tongue look extremely different yet share an **underlying similarity** in how their elements, relations and goals are organized. This is **going up Diotima's ladder**, from individual cases to the general principles they share.

sections.title: Motor primitives combine into a complex octopus action

teaching.text: **The octopus example comes from a 2023 Marine Biology paper by Jean Alupay, Jennifer Mather and Khalil Iskarous on the octopus arm slap.** An **Abdopus** octopus filmed in **tidal pools in Okinawa, Japan**, slapped at fish, and 19 slaps were analyzed in an **external reference frame** and an **animal-centered reference frame**.

**Each slap was built from two kinematic primitives, rotation and translation of the hydrostatic arms**, combined **serially** and **in parallel**. A **muscular hydrostat** has no bones and is supported by muscles pushing against each other, so the arm can bend anywhere along its length.
children: Combining a few primitives keeps movement flexible while controlling only a few **degrees of freedom**, independent ways of moving. The authors call this **flexible rigidity**.

teaching.text: **The slap supports Flash and Hochner's embodied organization view, and the idea that motor primitives combine syntactically**, by rules, the way words combine into sentences. The octopus combines **sensory feedback** about the moving fish with **feed-forward** pre-planned primitives, staying in **dynamic equilibrium** with its environment.

sections.title: Knowledge and other psychological skills in AI

teaching.text: **AI is a model of five animal psychological skills, knowing, recognizing, attending, acting and learning.** Knowing is stored information, recognizing is identifying what arrives, attending is focusing on what matters, acting is producing an output, and learning is changing knowledge from experience.

**The cloze procedure, introduced by Wilson Taylor in Journalism Quarterly in Fall 1953, measured one of these skills in humans.** Words are removed from a passage and readers fill the blanks. Predicting a word from the words around it is the same skill modern language AI performs.

sections.title: Inputs, knowledge, and a predicted distribution

teaching.text: **In GPT each word is a vector, a list of thousands of numbers, called an x or a token.** All of the AI's knowledge is stored in a few trillion numbers called **weights**, or **w's**, and the AI combines the W's with the x's using mostly **addition, subtraction, multiplication and division**.

**The calculations produce a probability distribution function over possible next words**, which all add up to one. For "chickens cackle and ducks," the tallest peak sits over **"quack."** The way the W's combine with the x's is itself a dynamical system, and learning is a simpler one, so it comes first.

sections.title: How initially random weights become useful

teaching.text: **The weights come from training that starts with no knowledge, summed up as "Fake it till you make it!"** The system starts with random W's, is given "chickens cackle and ducks," and predicts the next word. With random weights the peak may sit over "cat." The **target distribution** puts all the probability on "quack," so the system changes its W's to look more like the target. Repeated **billions of times** over more sequences, this is how LLMs learn and know.

sections.title: Random initialization and learning from mistakes

teaching.text: **AI learning depends on two tricks, shown in an image generated by ChatGPT.** **"Fake It Till You Make It"** means starting with random weights and predicting right away. **"Learn by Making Mistakes"** means each wrong prediction produces an **error** that is used to adjust the weights.

sections.title: A simple model of learning an average

teaching.text: **The average of 10, 12 and 14 is easy, 36 divided by 3 gives 12, but this formula does not work for speech, language, biological molecules and scenes.** For those, an estimate must be improved step by step.

**The AI method starts with a wild guess x and improves it through exposure to the data**, moving x a bit closer to each observed number in turn. This is **observation-based error learning**, the same logic as training an LLM with random weights corrected toward the right next word.

sections.title: Start from an arbitrary estimate

teaching.text: **SGD, stochastic gradient descent, learns the average, the essence, of [78, 67, 98, 85, 76, 68, 98, 72] one observation at a time.** The true average is 80.25, but SGD starts by picking a random estimate, 130 at **time 0**, written x[0]. The bracket is the **time step**.
**The learning rate γ is 25 percent**, the fraction of the error the estimate moves each step. At update 0 the estimate sits at 130 with the average far below it.

sections.title: An observation exposes a discrepancy

teaching.text: **One observation is enough to create error.** The first random pick is 98, so d[0] is 98. The **discrepancy**, or **loss**, is the estimate minus the observation, 130 minus 98, which is 32. The positive sign means the estimate is 32 too high, and since the average should be close to the data, the estimate needs to change.

sections.title: Correct a fraction rather than replacing the guess

teaching.text: **The correction subtracts 25 percent of the discrepancy.** A quarter of 32 is 8, so x[1] is 122. The estimate moves toward the observation but only a quarter of the way, which keeps any single observation from taking over.

sections.title: Correction after observation 2

teaching.text: **The procedure repeats with a new random observation each time.** On the second update the observation is 85, the discrepancy is 37, the correction is 9.25, and x[2] is 112.75.

sections.title: Correction after observation 3

teaching.text: **On the third update the observation is 76.** The discrepancy is 36.75, the correction is 9.1875, and x[3] is about 103.563.

sections.title: Correction after observation 4

teaching.text: **On the fourth update the observation is 68.** The discrepancy is 35.563, the correction is about 8.891, and x[4] is 94.672. Every observation so far has been below the estimate, so the estimate has fallen steadily, 130, 122, 112.75, 103.563, 94.672.

sections.title: A high observation pulls the estimate upward

teaching.text: **On the fifth update the observation, 98, is higher than the estimate of 94.672, so the discrepancy is negative, 3.328 below zero.** Subtracting 25 percent of a negative number is the same as adding, so the estimate rises to 95.504. The same rule moves the estimate toward the observation from either side, and the path bends upward for the first time.

sections.title: Correction after observation 6

teaching.text: **On the sixth update the observation is 72.** The discrepancy is 23.504, the correction is 5.876, and x[6] is 89.628.

sections.title: Correction after observation 7

teaching.text: **On the seventh update the observation is 78.** The discrepancy is 11.628, smaller now that the estimate is close to the data, the correction is 2.907, and x[7] is 86.721.

sections.title: Correction after observation 8

teaching.text: **On the eighth update the observation is 67, the lowest in the list.** The discrepancy is 19.721, the correction is about 4.930, and x[8] is 81.791, only about 1.5 above the true average.

sections.title: A high observation pulls the estimate upward

teaching.text: **On the ninth update 98 is drawn again, the third time, since random draws can repeat.** The discrepancy is negative 16.209, so the estimate rises from 81.791 to 85.843. A single high observation pushes the estimate away from the average, because each step responds only to the one observation drawn.

sections.title: Correction after observation 10

teaching.text: **On the tenth update the observation, 85, is extremely close to the estimate.** The discrepancy is 0.843, the correction is about 0.211, and the estimate barely moves, to 85.632.

sections.title: Correction after observation 11

teaching.text: **On the eleventh update the observation is 76.** The discrepancy is 9.632, the correction is 2.408, and x[11] is 83.224.

sections.title: Correction after observation 12

teaching.text: **On the twelfth update the observation is 68.** The discrepancy is 15.224, the correction is 3.806, and x[12] is 79.418, less than 1 below the true average of 80.25 after starting at 130.
children: Over all twelve updates the estimate went 130, 122, 112.75, 103.563, 94.672, 95.504, 89.628, 86.721, 81.791, 85.843, 85.632, 83.224 and 79.418. The path falls steeply, bumps upward twice when 98 is drawn, and ends up hovering near the average.

sections.title: Why the learning path jitters

teaching.text: **SGD has two steps, make an initial guess and use data to improve it.** **Stochastic** means a random observation is used each time. **Gradient** means the loss gives the direction, down for a positive discrepancy and up for a negative one. **Descent** means reducing the mistake.

**The path jitters, but its tendency is toward the average.** The random pushes up and down balance out over many updates. The same method applied to trillions of weights is how LLMs learn to predict the next word.

sections.title: An estimate can fall while its loss falls

teaching.text: **A second data set, [62, 70, 78, 82, 90, 98], with average 80, makes the link between estimate and loss easier to track.** The **mean motion of SGD** replaces the random observation with the average, so each new estimate is the old one minus 25 percent of its distance from 80.

**The loss is one half of the discrepancy squared.** Squaring makes the loss positive on either side of 80, and its rate of change as x changes is the discrepancy itself, which is why the discrepancy is the **gradient**.

**Starting at 140, the estimate goes 125, 113.75 and onward, while the loss goes 1800, 1012.5, about 569.5 and toward zero.** Each update keeps 75 percent of the discrepancy, the curve is smooth with no jitter, and the **estimate goes down as the loss goes down**.

sections.title: An estimate can rise while its loss falls

teaching.text: **With the same data and the same 25 percent rate but an initial condition of negative 100, the estimate rises toward 80**, to negative 55, then negative 21.25, reaching about 74 by update 12. The loss starts at 16200 and falls toward zero.
**The direction changes, but the learning does not.** From above, the estimate falls. From below, the estimate rises. In both cases the loss decreases, so learning is defined by the loss going down.

sections.title: Learning rate and starting condition

teaching.text: **Runs of 300 epochs from initial conditions of 130, 80 and 10 all settle around 80, and the learning rate decides how.** At **10 percent**, the runs reach 80 within 25 to 50 epochs and then wiggle between about 75 and 85. At **50 percent**, they arrive within a few epochs and then jump between about 70 and 95. At **1 percent**, they move slowly and smoothly and are still short of 80 after 300 epochs. At **80 percent**, they arrive at once and then jump between about 68 and 98, tracking individual data points.
children: The initial condition affects only the first part of each run.

sections.title: The learning tradeoff

teaching.text: **The learning rate creates a fundamental learning tradeoff.** Raising γ raises speed and lowers accuracy. Lowering γ lowers speed and raises accuracy. The 1 percent run is accurate but slow, and the 50 and 80 percent runs are fast but noisy.
**Thousands of people, for generations, have made their living finding ways to optimize learning** so that speed and accuracy both increase.

lecture04.title: 04 · Dynamic programming and shared physical principles

sections.title: Dynamical systems 1
Lecture agenda
A staged shortest-path problem

teaching.text: **The shortest path problem asks for the cheapest route through a network from a start to an end.** Each circle is a **state**, each arrow is a possible move, and each arrow carries a **cost**. The total cost of a route is the sum of its arrow costs.

**The network runs from A to J through stages**, A, then B and C, then D, E and F, then G, H and I, then J, so every route makes exactly four decisions. From A, B costs 12 and C costs 7. From B, D, E and F cost 5, 6 and 9, and from C they cost 14, 10 and 11. From D, G, H and I cost 8, 7 and 10, from E 9, 7 and 9, and from F 10, 7 and 8. G, H and I reach J for 5, 9 and 8.

**This is a model of decision-making over time.** Every choice has an immediate cost and also controls which future costs are available. A choice that looks good now can lock us into expensive moves later.

sections.title: Why the locally cheapest choice can lose

teaching.text: **A greedy algorithm takes the cheapest arrow out of the current state and never looks further ahead.** From A it takes C for 7, from C it takes E for 10, from E it takes H for 7, and from H it must pay 9 to reach J. The greedy route A, C, E, H, J costs 33, while A, B, D, G, J costs only 30 despite its expensive first move of 12.

**Greed is not good here.** The cheap move to C led into a part of the network where every continuation was costly, and the route ended at H with the large final cost of 9. Greed has no way of knowing about later costs.

**A tiny network makes this obvious.** The top route costs 10 then 10, and the bottom route costs 2 then 100. Greed picks 2 and pays 102 instead of 20. Writing inside each middle state the cost of the rest of the journey, 10 or 100, removes the blindness of greed.

sections.title: Blank source page
Exhaustive search trades speed for certainty

teaching.text: **An exhaustive algorithm lists every route, adds up each total, and picks the smallest, so its answer is guaranteed correct.** Here there are 2 times 3 times 3 times 1, or 18 routes, needing 54 additions and 18 comparisons.

**Its problem is how fast it grows.** Every added stage multiplies the number of routes, so with many stages and many states checking every route takes a very, very long time. Exhaustive search is accurate but impractical, and greedy search is fast but can be wrong. A method is needed that is both accurate and efficient.

sections.title: Bellman’s decomposition

teaching.text: **Bellman began with an imaginary step.** Imagine the best cost from B to J and from C to J were already known, and call them VBJ and VCJ. V stands for **Value**, the lowest total cost from a state to the goal.

**Then the best cost from A, VAJ, is one short calculation.** Through B the best total is 12 plus VBJ, and through C it is 7 plus VCJ. VAJ is the **minimum** of those two, written with min and braces. Each number in the set is one arrow cost plus the Value of the state the arrow leads to.

sections.title: Solve the smaller problems that supply the values

teaching.text: **The difficulty is that VBJ and VCJ are not known.** The rule for VAJ is correct but depends on two numbers not yet found.
**Bellman's strategy is to decompose a problem into subproblems you can solve.** Finding VAJ becomes finding VBJ and VCJ, and if those cannot be solved directly, they are broken down again.

sections.title: Propagating known costs backward

teaching.text: **The same reasoning applies at B.** If the best costs from D, E and F to J were known, VBJ would be the minimum of 5 plus VDJ, 6 plus VEJ and 9 plus VFJ, and VCJ the minimum of 14 plus VDJ, 10 plus VEJ and 11 plus VFJ.
**The Values of D, E and F depend in turn on G, H and I**, and at that stage the subproblems become trivial. Each of G, H and I has one arrow straight to J, so VGJ is 5, VHJ is 9 and VIJ is 8.
children: The rules form a chain from the end of the network back to the start. Information about the cost of reaching J travels **backward**, one stage at a time.

sections.title: Choose the best total after calculating values

teaching.text: **With G, H and I known, the Values are calculated stage by stage.** VDJ is the minimum of 13, 16 and 18, so 13. VEJ is 14 and VFJ is 15, all through G, whose small Value of 5 outweighs the arrow costs. VBJ is the minimum of 18, 20 and 24, so 18, and VCJ is the minimum of 27, 24 and 26, so 24. VAJ is the minimum of 12 plus 18 and 7 plus 24, so 30.

**Now go greedy on the Values, not the costs.** At A, B gives 30 and C gives 31, so go to **B** despite its expensive arrow. At B, D gives 18, so go to **D**. At D, G gives 13, so go to **G**, and then J. The best path is **A, B, D, G, J**, total 30.

**Dynamic programming is this two-part method.** Calculate the Values backward from the goal, then choose moves greedily using those Values. It needed one small minimum per state instead of adding up all 18 routes.

sections.title: A value summarizes the relevant future

teaching.text: **Dynamic programming is foresight about the whole route ahead.** From D, E or F the cheapest arrow is always the 7 into H, but H leads to something terrible, the final 9, so H has the largest Value in its stage. At E, H gives 7 plus 9, which is 16, while G gives 9 plus 5, which is 14. The Value of H warns about the 9 before we ever reach it, however many stages away it lies.

**The Values contain the future.** A late obstacle, the 9 out of H, made the early greedy choice of C a bad path. Because each Value already includes every obstacle ahead, going greedy on the Values makes present decisions optimal.
children: **Søren Kierkegaard** wrote that life can only be understood backwards but must be lived forwards. The Values are understood backwards, from the goal, and the decisions are lived forwards, from A.

sections.title: Recursive breakdown and reconstruction

teaching.text: **Dynamic programming poses a problem, its subproblems and its sub-subproblems, down to problems that are trivial.** VAJ needs VBJ and VCJ, which need VDJ, VEJ and VFJ, which need VGJ, VHJ and VIJ, which are just single arrow costs. Then the bigger problems are solved one level at a time back up to the original.

sections.title: The rule for propagating a value

teaching.text: **The Values are propagated from each stage to the stage before it by Bellman's rule.** The Value at one state is the minimum of a set of numbers, each the sum of the cost to one of the next states and the Value at that state. Start at the stage before the goal, apply the rule to each earlier stage in turn, and stop when A has its Value.
**Each Value is calculated once and reused by every state before it that connects to it**, such as VDJ of 13 feeding both the B rule and the C rule. That reuse keeps dynamic programming efficient.

sections.title: Least distance and least time can diverge

teaching.text: **Go through the bad 12 first to get onto a route that does not get stuck later at the 9.** It may seem to take a big brain to weigh the whole future against the present.

**A lifeguard faces the same trade-off.** On sand alone, running at a **constant speed**, the fastest route is the **shortest path**, a straight line. With the person in the water, running is fast and swimming is slow, so the **path of least time** runs farther along the sand and swims a shorter distance, bending at the water's edge. A longer run now cuts the costly swim later, like paying 12 early to avoid the 9.

sections.title: Refraction shares the least-time principle

teaching.text: **Decision-making is like physics, and light makes the same choice.** In **refraction**, light moves faster in air and slower in water, so its path bends at the surface just as the lifeguard's route bends, which is why a pencil in a glass of water looks broken at the water line.

**Light has no brain, yet it takes the least-time route**, so accepting an early cost to avoid a larger later one does not require a big brain. Physical systems find these optimal paths on their own, and dynamic programming describes the same kind of route through stages.

sections.title: Reading the completed state values

teaching.text: **Each state can be labeled with its Value and its best next state.** A is 30 and B. B is 18 and D, C is 24 and E. D is 13 and G, E is 14 and G, F is 15 and G. G, H and I are 5, 9 and 8, all to J. Following the labels from A gives A, B, D, G, J for 30.
**The labels give the best route from any state**, so from C the route is E, G, J for 24. One backward calculation solves the problem for every starting point at once.

sections.title: Pop quiz heading
Learning and coffee share approach to equilibrium

teaching.text: **A learning process plotted against epochs, with a 10 percent learning rate, settles near 80 from any initial condition.** Runs starting at 130, 80 and 10 meet within about 25 to 50 epochs and then fluctuate together in a narrow band. The change is fastest when x is far from 80 and slows as it gets closer.

**Coffee in a room at 18 degrees behaves the same way.** Hot cups starting at 100, 80 and 60 degrees cool toward 18, reaching about 29, 26 and 23 degrees after 8 minutes, and iced cups starting at 10, 5 and 0 degrees warm to about 16 or 17. The bigger the gap from room temperature, the faster the change.
**In both systems many starting values move toward the same final value**, and the speed of change depends on how far the current value is from it.

sections.title: Dynamical Systems 3
Homework reminder
Position and velocity change each other

teaching.text: **A harmonic oscillator is built from only two quantities, x and v.** The quantity x is how far something is displaced from its resting point, and v is its **velocity**, how fast and in which direction x is moving. The whole system is about **how x and v change each other over time**.
children: A dot over a variable means its change over time, in **Isaac Newton's notation**. A positive ẋ means x is rising, a negative ẋ means x is falling, and the size of ẋ says how fast. The same holds for v̇.

teaching.text: **The first rule is that ẋ equals v, so v steers x.** Whatever sign v has is the direction x moves. **The second rule is that v̇ equals minus x**, and the **minus sign** is the heart of the system. The quantity v is always pushed in the direction opposite to wherever x currently is.

sections.title: Read the sign of the change

teaching.text: **If v equals negative 5, then ẋ is negative 5, so x will go down.** The value of x does not matter for this. Only the sign of v decides whether x rises or falls.

**If x equals negative 5, then v̇ is minus negative 5, which is positive 5, so v will go up.** The two minus signs cancel. This is the restoring behavior in action, since an upward v then lifts x back toward zero.
children: The positive cases read the same way. A v of positive 5 makes x rise, and an x of positive 5 makes v fall. These are statements about the direction of change, so a velocity that is going up may still be negative, moving from a large negative value toward zero.

sections.title: Two different sign relationships

teaching.text: **The two rules treat the sign differently.** The rule ẋ equals v keeps the sign, so positive velocity makes position rise. The rule v̇ equals minus x reverses the sign, so positive position makes velocity fall.

**Whenever x moves away from zero, the second rule turns v around, and the first rule then carries x back toward zero.** This **restoring relationship** keeps the system swinging back and forth instead of drifting off. Keeping each quantity separate from its rate of change makes the motion understandable.

sections.title: Follow the position–velocity cycle

teaching.text: **Start with x at its highest positive value and v at zero.** Because x is positive, v drops below zero, so x starts to decrease, slowly at first. As v gets more negative, x falls faster. When x reaches zero, v̇ is zero, v is at its most negative, and x crosses zero at its fastest.
children: Once x is below zero, v̇ turns positive and v rises back toward zero while x keeps falling more slowly. When v returns to zero, x is at its lowest point and turns around. With x negative, v becomes positive, x climbs, v peaks as x crosses zero, and x returns to its maximum as v comes back to zero. Then the whole cycle repeats.

teaching.text: **Computing the system at a series of separate moments gives points that connect into two smooth waves.** The x wave starts at the top, and the v wave starts at zero and dips negative first. The two waves have the same shape but are shifted by a quarter of a cycle. The value v is at its extremes when x crosses zero, and v is zero when x is at its extremes.

sections.title: A closed feedback loop

teaching.text: **A dynamical system is a set of variables together with rules for how they change over time, and the x-v system is an oscillation or vibration dynamical system.** Oscillation and vibration both mean a quantity repeatedly swinging back and forth around a middle value.

**The relationship is a closed loop of influence.** One arrow runs from v to x for ẋ equals v, and another runs from x back to v for v̇ equals minus x. A change in v changes x, which changes v again, so once the system is set in motion it keeps cycling with nothing outside pushing it. Each cycle reaches the same height and depth and takes the same time.

sections.title: Homework reminder
Harmonic oscillators across systems

teaching.text: **The same structure of ẋ equals v and v̇ equals minus x shows up in the air of the vocal tract, the vocal folds, economies, music and matter itself.** Calling a system a harmonic oscillator means finding what plays the role of x, a displacement from rest, and what plays the role of v, its rate of change. It is a simplification, but it captures the basic back-and-forth pattern they all share.

sections.title: Compression and rarefaction of air

teaching.text: **A thin slice of air in the vocal tract contains many particles, and its pressure depends on how close together they are.** **High pressure** means the particles are very close together, and **low pressure** means they are very far apart. The particles stay the same in number and size. Only the spacing between them changes.

**Compression squeezes the particles closer than their equilibrium spacing, and rarefaction spreads them farther apart.** One pair of neighbors sits at 100 percent of its equilibrium distance at equilibrium, about 56 percent at the strongest compression, and about 141 percent at the strongest rarefaction. The slice cycles between these states, with real speech moving far less than these exaggerated values.

**The slice behaves like a harmonic oscillator.** The spacing relative to equilibrium plays the role of x. Squeezed air pushes itself apart and stretched air pulls itself back together, so any departure is pushed back toward equilibrium, the same restoring relationship as v̇ equals minus x.

sections.title: Connect air motion to a cosine

teaching.text: **The slice's motion follows a cosine, so x equals the cosine of the phase.** Here x is the **normalized expansion**, scaled so plus 1 is the largest stretch, maximum rarefaction, 0 is **equilibrium**, and minus 1 is the largest squeeze, maximum compression.

**The phase is the position within a cycle, and each 2π is one full cycle**, so 0 to 6π covers three cycles. At phase 0 the cosine is plus 1, at π over 2 it is 0, at π it is minus 1, at 3π over 2 it is 0 again, and at 2π it is back to plus 1. Values along the way, such as plus 0.74, minus 0.54, plus 0.31 or minus 0.21, say by their sign whether the slice is rarefied or compressed.
**This is the same wave the x-v system produces when x starts at its maximum and v at zero.** The vibrating air in the vocal tract follows the harmonic oscillator relationship.

sections.title: Vowels depend on tongue position

teaching.text: **Vowels differ in where the tongue sits inside the vocal tract**, as seen in MRI side views with the speaker facing left. Vowels are organized by **height**, **high** or **low**, and by **frontness**, **front**, **back** or **central**.
children: **"Dean"** is high and front. **"Dune"** is high and back. **"Dan"** is low and front. **"Don"** is low and back. **"Done"** is central, with the tongue resting in the middle of the mouth.

teaching.text: **Each tongue position gives the air a different shape, and a differently shaped column of air vibrates differently.** That difference in vibration is what makes one vowel sound different from another.

sections.title: Vowels combine more than one vibration

teaching.text: **A vowel is a sum of vibrations at several frequencies at once, so it can be modeled as harmonic oscillators added together.** **Frequency** is cycles per second in **hertz**, and a vibration at f hertz is the cosine of 2π times f times t.

**The vowel /i/ in "dean" is modeled as 1 Hz plus 4 Hz, the cosine of 2πt plus the cosine of 8πt**, a slow wave with fast ripples on top. **The vowel /a/ in "Don" is modeled as 2 Hz plus 3 Hz, the cosine of 4πt plus the cosine of 6πt**, whose close frequencies give a different pattern of tall and short swings.
children: These frequencies are example values, not measured ones, and the components have **equal amplitudes**, so each sum ranges between plus 2 and minus 2 and reaches plus 2 at 0, 1, 2 and 3 seconds. In between, the components partly cancel or reinforce, so /i/ can be at minus 1.21 while /a/ is at plus 0.58.

teaching.text: **Positive x still means rarefaction and negative x still means compression.** The two vowels squeeze and stretch the slice of air in two different time patterns, and those patterns distinguish them.

sections.title: Praat demonstration

teaching.text: **Praat is a free program for recording and analyzing speech.** It shows the **waveform**, air pressure changing over time, and breaks a sound into its frequencies. Recording "dean" and "Don" shows each vowel's repeating waveform made of several frequencies added together, the same idea as the two-frequency models.

sections.title: Two vibrating parts of speech

teaching.text: **Two things vibrate during speech, the air in the vocal tract and the vocal folds.** The **vocal folds** are two folds of tissue in the **larynx**. Air from the lungs pushes them apart, the pressure drops as air rushes through, and they come back together, many times per second.
children: Each opening lets through a puff of air, so the folds chop the airflow into rapid puffs. Those puffs set the vocal tract air vibrating, and the tongue's shaping of the tract sets which frequencies it vibrates at.

teaching.text: **A vowel is one oscillator driving another.** The folds are moving tissue, and the air is changing compression and rarefaction, so an explanation of speech must account for both.

sections.title: Economic cycles around a growth trend

teaching.text: **The business cycle, the repeated rise and fall of economic activity, is a harmonic oscillator.** It plots **time** against the **level of real output**, goods and services adjusted for price changes. Output moves from a **peak** through a **recession** to a **trough**, then through a **recovery** to the next peak.

**The swings happen around a rising trend line**, so each later peak can be higher than the one before. The distance of output above or below the trend plays the role of x. Above the trend output falls back, and below the trend it rises back, the same pattern as ẋ equals v and v̇ equals minus x.

sections.title: Meadows reading reminder
Music and vibration

teaching.text: **Music is built from harmonic oscillators.** Every note is a vibration at a particular frequency, whether from a plucked string, a column of air or a reed, and **pitch** corresponds to frequency. When several notes sound together their vibrations add, the way the 1 Hz and 4 Hz cosines add to form /i/.

sections.title: Atoms, shell pictures and wave modes

teaching.text: **At the scale of atoms, the harmonic oscillator appears as the quantum harmonic oscillator, whose energy is quantized**, meaning it can only take certain specific levels. Matter is made of atoms with different numbers of electrons, some vibrating at low frequency and some at high frequency, and electrons are **wave modes** rather than tiny balls on tracks.

**Magnesium shows two ways of drawing an atom.** It has 12 **electrons** and 12 **protons**, with ground-state configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s². The older **Bohr-style shell** drawing puts electrons on circular paths in shells of 2, 8 and 2. The **quantum orbital** description adds the **electron density** of each occupied orbital, 1s², 2s², 2p⁶ and 3s², into a total density, with darker shading where an electron is more likely to be found.
children: Orbitals are **quantized wave modes**, but **magnesium is not a harmonic-oscillator atom**. Real atoms follow related but different rules.

sections.title: Python position–velocity demonstration

teaching.text: **The x-v system can be computed step by step in Python.** Start with x at 1 and v at 0, and at each small step of size dt set ẋ equal to v and v̇ equal to minus x. The new x is the old x plus ẋ times dt, and the new v is the old v plus v̇ times dt. Smaller steps follow the true smooth waves more closely.

**The program uses numpy arrays, dt of 0.01 and 1000 steps, loops the two update lines, and plots x and v against t.** The output reproduces the oscillator. The value x traces a cosine from the top, and v starts at zero, drops negative first, and traces the same shape shifted by a quarter cycle.

sections.title: Dynamical Systems 5
Two quantities in an oscillator

teaching.text: **A harmonic oscillator has two variables that feed into each other, position x and velocity v.** A dot means change over time, so ẋ is the rate at which position changes and v̇ is the rate at which velocity changes.

**The first rule is that ẋ equals v, so velocity drives position.** Positive v makes x grow, negative v makes x shrink, and v of zero holds x still. This is the red arrow from v to x. **The second rule is that v̇ equals minus x, so position drives velocity with a minus sign.** Positive x pushes velocity down and negative x pushes it up. This is the blue arrow from x to v, and together the arrows form a **closed loop of mutual influence**.

**Stepping through from x at 1 and v at 0**, velocity turns negative, so position falls, slowly at first and then faster. When x crosses zero, v̇ is zero and velocity is at its most negative, so position is falling fastest. Below zero, v̇ turns positive and velocity climbs back, position bottoms out at negative 1 when velocity reaches zero, and the sequence runs in reverse back to plus 1.
children: Plotted against time, position and velocity are two waves offset by a quarter of a cycle. **Velocity is zero whenever position is at a peak or a trough, and largest whenever position is crossing zero.**

sections.title: Repeated change in a loop

teaching.text: **An oscillation, or vibration, is a repeating back-and-forth motion around a central point, and the x-v loop is the basic system that produces it.** The influence is **circular**, with no single cause at the start and no single effect at the end.

**The key property is that the system never comes to rest on its own.** Every time one variable reaches its target, the other is at its largest value and pushes it past the target again. Position overshoots zero because velocity is at its maximum there, and velocity overshoots zero because position is at its maximum there.

sections.title: Why a spring and a mass make vibration

teaching.text: **Vibration requires two physical effects working together.** The first is a **spring**, strictly a **viscous spring**, the springiness that returns things to a natural shape after a push or pull. Its **stiffness** is how strongly it pulls back. The second is **mass**, the amount of matter, which determines how an object carries motion once it is moving.

**Vibration shows up in many different systems.** It is the jolt from a car hitting a bump, it is music, it is boom and bust in economics, it is **oscillation in SGD**, where a trained value swings around its target, and it is the motion of the air in the vocal tract and of the vocal folds during speech.

sections.title: Air particles move closer and farther apart

teaching.text: **A slice of air in the vocal tract is many particles whose number and size stay the same. What changes is the distance between them.** At **equilibrium spacing** a chosen pair sits at 100 percent of its equilibrium distance.

**Compression pushes the particles closer than their resting distance**, to 56 percent for the chosen pair, and it is a high-pressure state. **Rarefaction spreads them farther apart**, to 144 percent, and it is a low-pressure state. During speech the slice alternates between the two around its equilibrium size, which is a vibration of the air. The sizes are exaggerated so the change is visible.

sections.title: Balancing feedback reduces displacement

teaching.text: **The spring effect alone is the rule that ẋ equals minus one third of x.** The rate of change is always one third of the current distance with the opposite sign, so positive x falls and negative x rises, both toward zero.
children: From an **initial condition** of 1, x drops by one third to two thirds, then by two ninths to four ninths, then by four twenty-sevenths to eight twenty-sevenths. Each drop is smaller than the one before.

teaching.text: **When x is smaller, its speed of falling is smaller too.** The curve starts steep and flattens as it nears zero, and it **never crosses zero**, since the speed shrinks to nothing as the distance does. From a negative start it rises toward zero the same way.

**The system has a natural resting condition at zero, and a discrepancy from it feeds back on itself to cancel that discrepancy.** This is **negative feedback**, also called **balancing feedback**, from Meadows. The change always opposes the discrepancy, and the system is in motion only to reach its **equilibrium**, where it has no reason to change further.
**The number minus one third is the stiffness.** A higher stiffness closes a bigger share of the remaining distance each step and returns faster. A lower stiffness returns more slowly.

sections.title: Mass carries motion onward

teaching.text: **If a mass is moving, it just keeps on moving.** A mass needs no discrepancy or target and has no natural resting position. **Galileo, Descartes and Newton** worked out that a mass in motion stays in motion, at **constant velocity**, covering the same distance in every equal interval of time, like a car rolling past the same amount of scenery each moment.
**This is exactly what the spring lacks.** A spring slows and stops at its resting point, while a mass carries its motion forward regardless of where it is.

sections.title: Returning to a place versus passing through it

teaching.text: **A spring stops at a place, while a mass stops after a process.** A spring alone on a table, with displacement x measured from its natural position at zero, returns from plus 1 and stops at zero **without crossing it**, and from negative 1 rises to zero without crossing it. The return curve flattens as it arrives, the same shape as the one-third rule.

**With a mass on the spring, the mass is moving fastest when it reaches zero and carries that motion through the crossing.** The spring then pulls it back from the other side, it stops near negative 1, and it is pulled back through zero again, through **every crossing**.
children: Graphed over time this is a **lightly damped oscillation**. **Damping** is the gradual loss of motion from the viscous part of the spring, so each swing is a little smaller, and the mass would come to rest only at the end of a long sequence of swings.

teaching.text: **Together the two effects recover the harmonic oscillator.** The spring supplies the pull back toward zero, v̇ equals minus x. The mass supplies persistent motion, ẋ equals v. A spring alone gives balancing feedback, a mass alone gives motion that never turns around, and **a spring and a mass together give vibration**.

sections.title: Air expansion follows a cosine

teaching.text: **The vibration of the air slice is described by a cosine, so x equals the cosine of the phase.** Here x is the **normalized expansion**, with plus 1 **maximum rarefaction**, 0 **equilibrium** and minus 1 **maximum compression**.

**The phase tracks where the slice is in its cycle, and each 2π is one cycle, so 0 to 6π is three cycles.** At 0 the slice is at maximum rarefaction, at π at maximum compression, and at 2π back at maximum rarefaction. In between, plus 0.84 is still rarefied and minus 0.84 is compressed but not at the tightest.

**This is the same wave position traced in the harmonic oscillator.** The springiness of the air pushes it back toward equilibrium spacing, and the mass of the air carries it past equilibrium each time. The model's sizes are exaggerated and its motion slowed.

sections.title: Compare tongue configurations for vowels

teaching.text: **Different vowels are made by placing the tongue in different positions**, seen in side-view MRI images during five words. Vowels are organized by **height** and by **front or back**.
children: **"Dean"** is high and front, with a wide open space in the throat behind the tongue. **"Dune"** is high and back, bunched toward the soft palate. **"Dan"** is low and front. **"Don"** is low and back, narrowing the space behind the tongue. **"Done"** is central, in the middle of the mouth.

teaching.text: **Each tongue position gives the air a different shape, which changes how it vibrates**, and those differences are what make one vowel sound different from another.

sections.title: Frequency counts cycles in a fixed interval

teaching.text: **Frequency is how many complete cycles a vibration goes through in a given time.** Three vibrations over the same 12 seconds all start at maximum rarefaction and cover the same range. The low-frequency one completes 3 cycles, 0.25 cycles per second. The mid-frequency one completes 6, 0.5 cycles per second. The high-frequency one completes 9, 0.75 cycles per second.

**All three reach the same extremes. The only difference is how quickly the cycle repeats.** Frequency is separate from how far the particles spread or squeeze. One cycle per second is **one hertz**, written **Hz**.

sections.title: Different combinations give different vowel patterns

teaching.text: **A vowel is a sum of vibrations at different frequencies happening at once in the same slice of air.** A cosine at f hertz is the cosine of 2π times f times t, so a 1 Hz vibration is the cosine of 2πt and a 4 Hz vibration is the cosine of 8πt. The model frequencies are small example values, not the actual frequencies of speech.

**The vowel /i/ in "dean" is modeled as 1 Hz plus 4 Hz.** The sum starts at plus 2, maximum rarefaction, ranges from plus 2 to minus 2, and is 0 at 0.5 seconds. The fast wave rides on the slow one, giving smaller wiggles inside each slow cycle, and the pattern repeats every second.

**The vowel /a/, close to the vowel in "Don," is modeled as 2 Hz plus 3 Hz.** It also starts at plus 2 and is 0 at 0.5 seconds, but between peaks it drops to a deep trough near minus 1.6, rises to a pair of small humps, and drops to another trough.

**Positive x is rarefaction and negative x is compression in both.** They start at the same value and repeat at the same rate, yet the air moves differently within each second. **The combination of frequencies is what distinguishes one vowel from another.**

sections.title: Predict the effect of mass and stiffness

teaching.text: **Perturbation theory studies how a system's behavior changes when a parameter, a fixed setting such as mass or stiffness, is nudged.** For a mass-spring system the behavior of interest is its **frequency**.

**Increasing the mass lowers the frequency**, because a heavier mass carries its motion more strongly and the spring takes longer to turn it around. **Increasing the stiffness raises the frequency**, because a stiffer spring pulls back harder and turns the mass around sooner. Knowing whether a system is heavy or light and stiff or loose predicts how it will vibrate.

sections.title: Hearing separates a mixture into frequencies

teaching.text: **The mass-spring relationships explain how the ear separates sounds by frequency**, the work of **Georg von Békésy**, **Nobel Prize in 1961**. The **basilar membrane** in the inner ear is wide at one end and narrow at the other. The **wide end** has large mass and small stiffness, heavy and loose. The **narrow end** has small mass and large stiffness, light and stiff.

**By perturbation theory, the wide end vibrates most for low-frequency sounds and the narrow end for high-frequency sounds**, with every point between tuned to an intermediate frequency. The membrane is a long row of mass-spring systems.

**Nerve fibers at each spot become active when that spot vibrates, telling the brain which frequencies are present.** A vowel built from two frequencies, like /i/, sets two different places vibrating, so the membrane separates the combination back into its components, which is how the ear tells /i/ from /a/.

sections.title: Learning rate trades speed for steadiness

teaching.text: **The learning rate γ sets how large each training update is, and an epoch is one full round through the training data.** Runs starting near 130, 80 and 10 head toward a target of about 80 over 300 epochs. At 1 percent they move smoothly but are still short of 80 at the end. At 10 percent they arrive within 30 to 50 epochs and wiggle only a little. At 50 percent they arrive in a few epochs but bounce between about 70 and 95. At 80 percent they bounce between about 68 and 97.

**This is the fundamental learning tradeoff.** Raising γ raises speed and lowers accuracy, because large updates keep throwing the value past the target so it oscillates around it. Lowering γ lowers speed and raises accuracy. This is the **oscillation in SGD** from the list of vibrations.
**Thousands of people, over generations, have made their living finding better ways to optimize**, so that speed and accuracy increase together.

sections.title: Dynamical Systems 6
Exam reminder
A spring alone and a mass–spring system

teaching.text: **A spring stops at a place, but a mass stops after a process.** The **displacement x** is how far the end of the spring is from its **natural position**, x at 0, with a stretch at plus 1 and a squeeze at minus 1.

**A spring alone, pulled to plus 1 and released, pulls itself back and stops exactly at zero.** The curve drops quickly, then more slowly, and never crosses zero, because the pull shrinks as the stretch shrinks. Pushed to minus 1, it rises to zero and never goes above it. A massless spring **stops at a place**.

**With a mass attached, the mass shoots right through zero.** It is moving fast when it gets there, compresses the spring on the other side, stops near minus 1, and is pushed back through zero again. **The mass carries motion through every crossing**, and x makes a wave, an **oscillation**.

**Each swing is slightly smaller than the last, a lightly damped oscillation.** **Damping** is anything that drains motion, such as friction, so the mass **stops after a process** of many crossings. A mass-spring system has a **frequency**, cycles per second. A massless spring has none.

sections.title: Mass, stiffness and the frequencies of speech

teaching.text: **Perturbation theory asks what happens when one setting of a system is nudged.** For a mass-spring system the settings are the **mass m** and the **stiffness k**, and the behavior is the frequency f. **Increasing the mass decreases the frequency**, since a heavier mass is harder to speed up and slow down, so each swing takes longer. **Increasing the stiffness increases the frequency**, since a stiffer spring pulls back harder and each swing finishes sooner. Only the direction matters, not the exact number.

**Speaking changes the effective mass and stiffness of air in the vocal tract.** Moving the tongue, jaw and lips squeezes some portions of the air in the tube and opens others, so each portion acts more or less like a mass or a spring. Set vibrating by the vocal folds, the air vibrates at **many frequencies at once**, and the set depends on **where** and **how much** the air is squeezed, so each vowel and consonant has its own.
children: MRI images of **dean, dune, done, Dan** and **Don** show the different squeezes. Dean is high and forward, dune high and back with the lips forward, done in the middle, Dan low and front, and Don low and back, squeezing the throat. Each shape gives a different set of frequencies.

teaching.text: **The listener has to recover these frequencies from the sound.** The ear must find which low, middle and high frequencies are present and how strong each is, so the brain can tell **"scene"** from **"son."** How the ear does this is answered by the inner ear.

sections.title: The cochlea connects incoming sound to neural signals

teaching.text: **Sound is a wave of vibration in the air.** It arrives at the **external ear** and travels inward through the ear canal to the **inner ear**. The **cochlea**, the one name to know, is a small coiled tube like a snail shell deep in the skull. It sends the brain signals saying which frequencies are present.

**The inner ear has two regions.** The upper one holds the **semicircular ducts**, the **utricle** and **saccule**, and the **cristae** in their **ampullae**, which are not the parts that separate frequencies. The lower one is the cochlea, with the **vestibular, cochlear** and **tympanic ducts** spiraling together inside it. Soft tubes, the **membranous labyrinth**, sit inside the hollows of the **bony labyrinth**, and the **vestibulocochlear nerve** carries the signals to the brain.

sections.title: The path into the basilar membrane

teaching.text: **Sound reaches the cochlea through a chain.** It strikes the **tympanic membrane**, the eardrum, which moves the **malleus**, which moves the **incus**, which moves the **stapes**. The stapes pushes in and out on the fluid inside the cochlea.

**The basilar membrane runs the length of the cochlea**, from the stapes end to the tip of the coil, the **helicotrema**. When the stapes pushes on the fluid, the fluid makes the basilar membrane vibrate, and the membrane turns that vibration into information about frequency.

sections.title: Frequency is represented by place and nerve activity

teaching.text: **The basilar membrane is wide and heavy at the helicotrema end and narrow and stiff at the stapes end.** The wide end has **large mass** and **small stiffness**, heavy and floppy. The narrow end has **small mass** and **large stiffness**, light and stiff.

**Each spot acts like its own mass-spring system, so frequency increases steadily along the membrane.** Large mass and small stiffness both lower the frequency at the floppy end, so it vibrates at **low frequencies**. Small mass and large stiffness both raise it at the stiff end, so it vibrates at **high frequencies**.

**A sound with many frequencies is sorted out by place.** Each frequency shakes the part of the membrane tuned to it. **Neurons** attached along the membrane signal **to the brain**, which tells the frequencies by **which neurons are active** and their strength by how strongly they signal. One pattern is "scene," another is "son." **Georg von Békésy won the Nobel Prize in 1961** for this mechanism.

sections.title: How vocal folds make and change pitch

teaching.text: **The vocal folds are two small muscles, about 1 cm long and 1 mm high, sitting across the airway.** Muscle has mass and stiffness, so the folds behave like a mass-spring system. About **10 other muscles** can **stretch** them, making them **stiffer** and raising the frequency, or **bunch** them, making them **effectively heavier** and lowering it.

**Controlling the frequency gives musical notes in singing, conveys questions, mistrust, belief, surprise and emotion in English, and distinguishes word meanings in tone languages.** The frequency is called **pitch**, F0, the **fundamental frequency**.

**Pressure from the lungs blows the closed folds apart, and the air rushing through sucks them back together**, like a shower curtain pulled toward the water. That suction is the **Bernoulli force**, which also lifts airplanes. Pressure builds again, and the cycle repeats **hundreds of times per second**, each cycle one vibration.

sections.title: Position-first updates keep the oscillator bounded

teaching.text: **A harmonic oscillator is a mass on a spring with no damping, described by ẋ equals v and v̇ equals minus k over m times x.** The dot means rate of change. The first rule says position changes at the velocity. The second says velocity is pushed back toward zero, harder for a stiffer spring and less for a heavier mass, so k over m holds both parts of perturbation theory.

**With k over m at 1, a time step Δt of 0.5, and a start at x of 1 and v of 0, each step updates x first and then v using the new x.** The new x is the old x plus Δt times the old v, and the new v is the old v minus Δt times the new x. This is **position-first symplectic Euler**, and the order matters.
children: Step 1 gives x of 1.000 and v of minus 0.500. Step 2 gives x of 0.750 and v of minus 0.875. Step 3 gives x of 0.3125, shown as 0.313, and v of about minus 1.031. Later steps use the full-precision numbers.

teaching.text: **After 12 steps, x falls through zero, bottoms out at minus 1.022 at step 7, and climbs back to 0.920, while v drops to minus 1.031 at step 3, crosses zero near step 6, and peaks at 1.019 at step 9.** The mass is fastest through zero and slowest at its farthest point, and the swing stays near a size of 1.
children: These values are an approximation from stepping in chunks of 0.5. In Python the loop appends the new position, then the velocity update reads x[-1], which is now the **new x**.
