sections.title: Masses and Springs in Speech Production
Mass, stiffness, position, and frequency

teaching.text: Every vibrating system in speech follows a small set of principles, and each one connects to the others.
children: **Raising the mass lowers the frequency, and raising the stiffness raises the frequency.**
**A system with n masses has n modes**, and each higher mode has a higher frequency, because more parts go against each other and more springs stretch and compress.

**An increase in mass lowers frequency in proportion to how much that mass moves**, and **an increase in stiffness raises frequency in proportion to how much that spring stretches and compresses.** Both depend on where the change is made.
**Where there is maximal movement there is no stretching, and where there is maximal stretching there is no movement.**

In a **fixed-fixed system**, the frequencies are called **harmonics** and are **whole-number multiples** of the base frequency, and in a **fixed-free system** they are called **formants** and are **odd multiples**.

teaching.text: If the mass and the stiffness of a system are both raised, it might seem the two effects simply **cancel out**. That is only true for a **single mass on a single spring**. In a system with many masses and springs, a spot that is moving a lot is hardly stretching, and a spot that is stretching a lot is hardly moving, so only one of the two changes matters at that spot.
children: Picture a spot on a string that never moves but is stretched hard. Extra mass there does nothing, while extra stiffness raises the frequency, so the frequency goes up.
Picture a spot that swings up and down the most. Extra stiffness there does nothing, while extra mass slows it down, so the frequency goes down.

sections.title: One more mass, one more mode

teaching.text: Adding masses adds modes, and the same shapes keep repeating. **Mode 1** always has everything moving together, **Mode 2** always splits the system into two halves going against each other, and **Mode 3** always has the middle going against the sides.
children: The more the parts go against each other, the more the springs work, so **higher modes are stiffer and faster**. In plain terms, a higher mode is not made of stiffer springs. It just makes the same springs do more stretching.

sections.title: Why fixed–fixed frequencies are integer multiples

teaching.text: In a string fixed at both ends, the first mode is **one half-wave**, a single bump that goes from no motion at one end, to the most motion in the middle, to no motion at the other end. Each higher mode packs **more of these half-wave packets** into the same length.
children: **Mode 2 holds two packets**, with one half going up while the other half goes down. Each packet behaves like a copy of Mode 1, so Mode 2 has **twice the stiffness** and **twice the frequency**.
**Mode 3 holds three packets**, and **Mode 5 holds five**, so the fifth mode has five times the frequency of the first.
The short version for an exam answer is that **the fifth mode has the first mode fitted into it five times**, so it has five times the stiffness and five times the frequency.

teaching.text: The numbers do not have to start at 100. A voice whose base frequency is **250 hertz** has its next harmonics at 500, 750 and 1000 hertz, because each one is still a whole number of copies of the first.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics

teaching.text: A string fixed at both ends vibrates in all of these modes at once, and its **spectrum**, with **frequency** along the bottom and **amplitude** going up, has **evenly spaced spikes**, one for each harmonic. If the first harmonic is 100 hertz, the next ones are 200, 300, 400 and 500 hertz.
children: The **vocal folds** are fixed on all sides, just behind the Adam's apple, so they behave like this kind of fixed-fixed system and produce harmonics.

sections.title: A membrane combines spatial modes

teaching.text: The vocal folds form a **membrane**, and the same packet counting works on a surface. The first mode is a single bump across the whole membrane, the second mode squeezes two of those bumps in, so it has twice the frequency, and the fourth mode squeezes in four ups and downs, so it has four times the frequency.

sections.title: One fixed end and one free end

teaching.text: A **building** is **fixed at the bottom** and **free at the top**. In high winds or an earthquake, engineers want it to sway only in **Mode 1**, all together, which is mildly unpleasant on a high floor but safe. A higher mode would send some floors one way and other floors the other way, and the whole structure could shatter.

A string can be set up the same way, fixed at the bottom and free at the top. Its first mode is not a full half-wave anymore. It goes from **no motion at the fixed end** to **lots of motion at the free end**, which is only **one quarter of a wave**.

sections.title: Why fixed–free frequencies are odd multiples

teaching.text: In a fixed-free system, each mode is built from **quarter-wave packets**, and each packet runs from no motion to lots of motion. **Mode 1 holds one packet**, **Mode 2 holds three**, **Mode 3 holds five** and **Mode 4 holds seven**, so with a base of 100 hertz the modes come at 100, 300, 500 and 700 hertz.

**Two packets can never fit.** Stacking two quarter-wave packets gives no motion, then lots of motion, then no motion again, which puts a still point at the top as well as the bottom and makes the system **fixed at both ends**. Adding one more packet, for **three** in total, ends with lots of motion at the top again, so that is the next possible mode.
children: The simple version is that the free end must always be moving, and only an odd number of quarter-waves lands on a moving end.

teaching.text: The frequencies of a fixed-free system are called **formants**. **A formant is a frequency of vibration of a system that is fixed on one side and completely free on the other**, and formants are **odd multiples** of the lowest one, written **F1**, **F2** and **F3**.

sections.title: Count quarter-waves from the boundary conditions

teaching.text: Counting quarter-wave packets gives every formant from the first. If **F1 is 500 hertz**, then **F2 is three times that, 1500 hertz**, and **F3 is five times that, 2500 hertz**.
children: Each step between formants is twice the first formant, because each new mode adds two more quarter-wave packets.

sections.title: Air in a fixed–free tube has modes

teaching.text: The air inside the mouth and throat forms a tube. At one end are the **vocal folds**, and because they are closed, the air there **cannot go back and forth**, so that end is **fixed**. At the other end the **lips are open**, so the air can go back and forth freely, and that end is **free**.
children: So **the motion of air in the vocal tract is like a building**, and the math describing them is almost exactly the same, and its frequencies are **formants**.
Speaking changes the stiffness and mass of the air in different parts of the tract, which moves the formants, and that is how listeners hear different vowels and consonants.

sections.title: Compression and motion alternate in an air column

teaching.text: The air in the tube can be modeled as lines of particles, where each particle stands for billions of air molecules.
children: Where the lines come **really close together and then really far apart**, the air is compressing and stretching, so it is acting like a **spring**.
Where the lines just **move back and forth** without changing their distance, the air is acting like a **mass**, which is easiest to see at the **free end at the lips**.
An easy way to read it is that bunching and spreading means springiness, and sliding without bunching means mass.

teaching.text: The air's modes match a building's modes. In **Mode 1**, the only point of no motion is the fixed end, in **Mode 2** there are **two**, and in **Mode 3** there are **three**, and around each of them there is lots of compression and expansion.

In **Mode 4** of a building, **the most springiness is at the fixed bottom and at the three points where the building's line crosses its resting position**, four places in all, because those points do not move.
children: Raising the stiffness at a place of maximal movement changes **nothing**, because the structure is not acting like a spring there, while raising it at a place of no movement makes the frequency **shoot up**.

sections.title: Vowel shape locates a constriction

teaching.text: A **constriction** is a place where the tongue or lips squeeze the air, measured from the **glottis**, the tiny space between the vocal folds at the fixed end.
children: In **done**, the central vowel, there is **no constriction**.
In **dean**, a **front high vowel**, the air is squeezed under the roof of the mouth, about **two thirds of the way from the glottis**.
In **Don**, a **low back vowel**, the air is squeezed far back, about **one third of the way from the glottis**.
In **dune**, a **back high vowel**, the lips are rounded close together, which squeezes the air **at the lips**, and **Dan** is a **front low vowel**.

sections.title: Why a constriction can raise one formant and lower another

teaching.text: **Compressing air raises its stiffness**, just as squeezing a tire makes it stiffer, so a constriction at a place that experiences lots of compression **raises frequency**. **Bunching up air raises its mass**, because it raises the air's **density**, so a constriction at a place where the air moves a lot **lowers frequency**.

So every constriction **increases both mass and stiffness**, but that does not mean constrictions have no effect on frequency. **The parts of a vibrating medium that move the most alternate with the parts that compress and expand the most.**
children: A useful way to answer any constriction question is to ask two things in order. First, is the air at this spot mostly moving or mostly compressing in this mode? Second, which change counts there, the extra mass or the extra stiffness?

teaching.text: The same two-step reasoning answers a question about a string fixed at both ends. Take a small spot where **Mode 3 crosses its middle line** while **Mode 4 is at the top of a bump**, and raise both the mass and the stiffness of that spot.
children: In **Mode 3**, the string does not move at that spot but is stretched the most, so only the extra stiffness counts, and **Mode 3's frequency goes up**.
In **Mode 4**, the string moves the most at that spot and hardly stretches, so only the extra mass counts, and **Mode 4's frequency goes down**.

sections.title: Compression and motion alternate in an air column

teaching.text: Before reasoning about any vowel, it helps to know where the air moves and where it compresses in the first two modes.
children: In **Mode 1**, the air near the closed glottis end compresses and expands a lot, and the air near the open lip end just moves back and forth.
In **Mode 2**, the air compresses a lot at the closed end and again at a second region about two thirds of the way along, and in between, about one third of the way along, it mostly moves.
**The closed end is always springy and the open end is always massy, in every mode**, because air can be squeezed against a closed end but has nothing to squeeze against at an open end.

sections.title: Air in a fixed–free tube has modes

teaching.text: The mass-spring chain marks the three vowel locations along the tube, **one third of the way from the glottis** for **/a/**, **two thirds of the way** for **/i/**, and the **lip end** for **/u/**. Each vowel adds mass and stiffness at its own spot, and the effect on F1 and F2 depends on whether the air there is moving or compressing in each mode.

Adding mass and stiffness at the **very top of a building** lowers the frequency of **every mode**, including Mode 4. The top is the free end, so in every mode it has the most motion and almost no springiness, and only the extra mass counts there.
children: **The top of the building corresponds to the lip end of the vocal tract**, which is why rounding the lips lowers every formant.

sections.title: /u/ loads the moving lip end

teaching.text: **/u/** rounds the lips, which squeezes the air at the **free end**. The free end moves a lot and hardly compresses in both Mode 1 and Mode 2, so the extra **mass** counts in both, and **F1 and F2 both go down**.
children: A speaker who moved from the central vowel into /u/ produced exactly this, with **both formants dropping** in the recording.

sections.title: /i/ has opposite effects on F1 and F2

teaching.text: **/i/** squeezes the air about **two thirds of the way from the glottis**.
children: In **Mode 1**, that spot has lots of motion, so the extra mass counts and **F1 goes down**.
In **Mode 2**, that spot has lots of compression, so the extra stiffness counts and **F2 goes up**.
A speaker who moved from the central vowel into /i/ showed the **first formant dropping a lot** and the **second formant going up**.

sections.title: /a/ reverses the two effects

teaching.text: **/a/** squeezes the air about **one third of the way from the glottis**, which reverses the /i/ pattern.
children: In **Mode 1**, that spot near the fixed end compresses a lot, so the extra stiffness counts and **F1 goes up**.
In **Mode 2**, that spot moves a lot, so the extra mass counts and **F2 goes down**.

teaching.text: The reasoning also runs backward. **If a constriction raises a formant a great deal, the air at that spot must be very springy and hardly moving in that mode**, and **if a constriction lowers a formant a great deal, the air at that spot must be moving a lot**.

sections.title: Compression and motion alternate in an air column

teaching.text: A measured **schwa**, made with no constriction, had formants near **500, 1500 and 2500 hertz**, which are the odd multiples a uniform fixed-free tube predicts. Every vowel moves these formants away from the schwa values by changing where the air moves and where it compresses.

sections.title: The source supplies harmonics and the filter shapes their heights

teaching.text: Speech combines **two vibrating systems at the same time**.
children: The **vocal folds** are a fixed-fixed system, so they are the **source** and produce **harmonics**. The lowest harmonic is called the **base frequency**, or **F0**, and here the harmonics are **100 hertz apart**.
The **air in the vocal tract** is a fixed-free system, so it acts as a **filter**, and its frequencies are the **formants**. For the schwa, the formants sit near **500, 1500, 2500 and 3500 hertz**.

teaching.text: **The formants shape the heights of the harmonics.** The harmonics are all still there, but **harmonics near a formant are tall, and harmonics far from any formant are short**, so the outline of their heights, called the **envelope**, rises into a peak at each formant.
children: **The harmonics stay the same from vowel to vowel, but their heights change, and the envelope is what makes the vowel.**
In plain terms, the vocal folds decide which frequencies are present, and the shape of the mouth decides which of them are loud.

sections.title: The /i/ filter keeps F1 low and F2 high

teaching.text: For **/i/**, the filter keeps **F1 low and F2 high**. The tall harmonics are bunched at the very bottom of the spectrum, then a long stretch of short harmonics follows, and the next tall group appears much higher up, so the two lowest formants are **far apart**.

sections.title: The /a/ filter raises F1 and lowers F2

teaching.text: For **/a/**, the filter **raises F1 and lowers F2**. The first two groups of tall harmonics sit **close together** in the lower part of the spectrum.
children: The same source harmonics are under both /i/ and /a/. Only the filter differs, and moving the constriction is what moves the formants and reshapes which harmonics are loud.

sections.title: A spectrogram places successive spectra in time

teaching.text: **A spectrum describes one instant**, but speech is **time-varying**, because the vocal tract keeps moving and constrictions are made and unmade. **A spectrogram stacks many spectra side by side over time.**
children: **Time** runs along the **horizontal axis**.
**Frequency**, which was the horizontal axis of each spectrum, becomes the **vertical axis**.
**Amplitude**, which was the height of each spike, becomes **darkness**, so the louder a frequency is, the darker it looks.

teaching.text: The formants appear as **dark bands** that move as the speaker moves. In **/ia/**, the two lowest bands start **far apart** during /i/, and as the speaker moves into /a/, **F1 rises and F2 falls**, so the bands **come close together**.

sections.title: Reflection prompt

teaching.text: **Where were you a year ago?** is a good sentence for seeing source and filter working together over time. The vocal folds, as the source, keep producing harmonics, while the vocal tract, as the filter, keeps changing shape, so the envelope over the harmonics changes from moment to moment.
children: On a spectrogram, these changes show up as **dark bands that rise and fall**, since the dark bands are the formants and darkness shows amplitude.
Where the vowel sounds like **/i/**, the two lowest bands spread far apart, and during **you**, all the bands drop because the lips are rounded.

teaching.text: **A spectrum shows one frozen instant, but a spectrogram shows how the formants move**, and real speech is all movement. Reading a sentence like this one means following each band and asking what constriction moved it.

sections.title: Wide harmonic spacing makes formants harder to identify

teaching.text: Formants can only show up through the harmonics, so the spacing of the harmonics matters. With harmonics every **100 hertz** and formants at **300 and 2100 hertz**, **many harmonics** sit under each formant peak, so the formants are easy to see.

With a higher base frequency, such as **250 hertz**, fewer harmonics land on each formant peak and a formant can fall **between two harmonics**, so **it becomes very hard to tell the harmonics from the formants**.
children: A **toddler's** harmonics can be at 400, 800 and 1200 hertz, and a **soprano's** can start at 800 hertz, which is why their vowels can be very hard to identify.

teaching.text: **Formants are the smooth envelope, and harmonics are samples of it.** A higher F0 means fewer samples, so the spectrogram stops looking like clean formant bands.
children: A simple way to see it is that the harmonics are like the points used to trace a curve. With many points the curve is obvious, and with only a few points it is hard to see.

sections.title: Homework 4 lab reminder
Speech → Neural Networks
Five membrane modes combine into one motion

teaching.text: Speech uses **two major vibrating systems**. The first is the **vocal folds**, a **membrane** that is **fixed on all sides** and made of a whole bunch of masses and springs. It vibrates in many modes at once, with all the masses going up and down together in Mode 1, half going up while the other half goes down in Mode 2, and more complicated patterns above that, and all five modes add together into one combined motion.
children: Because the vocal folds are a fixed-fixed system, their frequencies are **harmonics**, which are whole-number multiples of the lowest one.
The **bottom-most harmonic** is called **F0**. Each person has a different F0, but the other harmonics are always its multiples.

sections.title: A fixed end and a free end select odd harmonics

teaching.text: The second system is the **air in the vocal tract**. It is **fixed at the glottis**, because the closed vocal folds keep the air there from moving back and forth, and it is **free at the lips**, where the air can go in and out. A fixed end and a free end select only the **odd harmonics**, so its frequencies are one, three, five and seven times the lowest one.

sections.title: Quarter-wavelength packets explain the allowed modes

teaching.text: Each fixed-free mode is built from **quarter-wavelength packets**, each running from no motion at a still point to the most motion at a moving point. **Mode 1 holds one packet, Mode 2 holds three, Mode 3 holds five and Mode 4 holds seven.**
children: Two packets would end with a still point at the free end, which is impossible, so only odd numbers of packets fit, and that is why the formants are odd multiples of the first.

sections.title: Air moves longitudinally in vocal-tract modes

teaching.text: In the vocal tract, the air moves **longitudinally**, back and forth along the tube, not up and down. Each formant is one mode of this longitudinal motion, with F1 the lowest mode and F2 the next.
children: The modes look like the building's modes turned on their side, with the fixed glottis end at the left and the free lip end at the right.

sections.title: Track air motion separately from compression

teaching.text: **The closed end is always springy and the open end is always massy, in every mode.** Air can be squeezed against a closed end, but there is nothing to squeeze against at an open end.
children: Near the **closed end**, the slivers of air come very close together and then far apart, so the air **compresses and expands** and acts like a **spring**.
Near the **open end**, the slivers stay equally far apart and simply go back and forth, so the air acts like a **mass**.
In plain terms, the lip end swings like a heavy door, and the throat end squeezes like a pillow.

teaching.text: In higher modes, springy places and massy places **alternate** more and more times along the tube.

sections.title: Compare positions within an air mode

teaching.text: A constriction can be judged at any spot, in any mode, with the same chain of reasoning. Take a spot inside the tube where, in **Mode 3**, the lines of air are bunching up and spreading apart while hardly moving back and forth. Constricting the tract at that spot raises **F3**.
children: The first step is that constricting air always **increases both its mass and its stiffness**, just as squeezing a tire makes it stiffer.
The second step is that at this spot in Mode 3, the air is acting like a **pure spring**, with compression and expansion but no movement back and forth, so the extra mass does not matter.
The third step is that only the extra stiffness counts, and **raising stiffness raises frequency**, so **F3 goes up**.

teaching.text: The answer is never memorized. It is **built one claim at a time**, with each claim resting on the one before it, which is the same way any good argument is built in science or in art.

sections.title: Vowel positions change where the tract is narrowed

teaching.text: Images taken while people speak show where each vowel squeezes the air in the tube that runs from the closed glottis to the open lips.
children: The vowel in **done** has **no constriction** at all.
**dean** squeezes the air near the front, about **two thirds of the way from the glottis**.
**Don** squeezes the air far back in the throat, about **one third of the way from the glottis**.
**dune** squeezes the air **at the lips** by rounding them, and **Dan** is a low front vowel.

sections.title: A constriction changes inertia and restoring stiffness

teaching.text: A constriction changes both the **inertia** of the air, which is its mass, and its **restoring stiffness**. In the mass-spring model, a constriction is drawn as **heavier masses and stiffer springs** at that spot.
children: It always raises both, but because moving places and springy places alternate, **its effect depends on what the air is doing there in each mode**.
**Whenever stiffness is what matters at a spot, the frequency goes up, and whenever mass is what matters, the frequency goes down.**

sections.title: Use both modes to interpret the same tract location

teaching.text: The same location in the tube can act differently in the two modes, so both modes have to be checked separately. A spot can be massy in Mode 1 and springy in Mode 2, and then one constriction lowers F1 while raising F2.
children: That is why a vowel is defined by the pair of formants, not by one formant alone.

sections.title: Lip loading lowers both F1 and F2 in the /u/ model

teaching.text: **/u/** squeezes the air at the lips. At the open end the air goes back and forth with hardly any compression in **every** mode, so the air there is a pure mass. The extra stiffness does not matter, the extra mass does, and **F1 and F2 both go down**.
children: Compared with schwa's reference values of about **500 and 1500 hertz**, a measured /u/ had an F1 down in the low two hundreds, well below 500.

sections.title: A front constriction separates the effects on F1 and F2

teaching.text: **/i/** squeezes the air about two thirds of the way from the glottis.
children: In **Mode 1**, the air there moves back and forth, so it acts like a mass, the extra mass counts, and **F1 goes down**.
In **Mode 2**, the air there compresses and expands, so it acts like a spring, the extra stiffness counts, and **F2 goes up**.
A speaker moving from schwa into /i/ showed exactly this, with **F1 going down and F2 going up**.

sections.title: A back constriction reverses the F1 and F2 pattern

teaching.text: **/a/** squeezes the air about one third of the way from the glottis.
children: In **Mode 1**, that spot is close enough to the closed end that the air is mostly springy, so the extra stiffness counts and **F1 goes up**.
In **Mode 2**, that spot sits between two springy regions, so the air there is mostly moving, the extra mass counts, and **F2 goes down**.
A speaker producing /a/ showed **F1 going up and F2 going down**, and a typical /a/ has its F1 and F2 fairly close together.

sections.title: Air motion and compression in the vocal-tract modes

teaching.text: Across all three vowels, the logic is the same. **Find whether the air at the constriction is mostly moving or mostly compressing in each mode, then decide whether the extra mass or the extra stiffness counts.**
children: At the lips, the air is massy in both modes, so /u/ lowers both formants.
Two thirds along, the air is massy in Mode 1 and springy in Mode 2, so /i/ lowers F1 and raises F2.
One third along, the air is springy in Mode 1 and massy in Mode 2, so /a/ raises F1 and lowers F2.

sections.title: The vocal-fold source sets harmonic spacing

teaching.text: The vocal folds are the **source**, and their mass and stiffness set **F0** and therefore the spacing of the harmonics.
children: **Big, heavy, loose vocal folds** have a large mass and small stiffness, so their **F0 is low**, around 100 hertz, with harmonics at 200, 300 and so on.
**Tighter, lighter vocal folds** have a higher F0, such as 250 hertz, and **very tight, light vocal folds** have an even higher F0, such as 350 hertz.

teaching.text: **F0 is not fixed while people talk.** Speakers keep changing F0 by tightening and loosening the vocal folds, and listeners use those changes to get meaning.
children: **The dog slept here** said as a statement has F0 falling at the very end, while the same words as a question have F0 rising at the end.
The way F0 moves also tells listeners whether a person is being sarcastic, pretending, or even lying.

sections.title: The vocal-tract filter favors nearby harmonics

teaching.text: The air in the vocal tract is the **filter**, and its formants depend on **where the constriction is**. Schwa has F1 near 500 and F2 near 1500, /u/ has lower formants, /i/ has F1 and F2 very far apart, and /a/ has them very close together.
**The core rule is that a formant encourages the closest harmonics to be audible, and harmonics far from that formant are muted.**
children: **The vowel shape is the filter. The voiced source supplies the harmonics, and the filter chooses which harmonics survive.**

sections.title: One filter can look different at different pitches

teaching.text: **The lower F0 is, the more harmonics the formants can shape.** With harmonics every 100 hertz, many harmonics sit under each formant, so the shaped spectrum traces the formant peaks smoothly.
With very light, tight vocal folds, a formant at 500 hertz may have **no harmonic near it to amplify**, so sparse harmonics can miss a formant or make it look ambiguous.
children: An **opera singer** is an extreme case, which is why sung vowels are hard to identify, and singers are even trained to shape the mouth so the formants line up with the harmonics.
A **small child** has an F0 near 500 hertz, so very few harmonics fall near the formants, and only caretakers used to the child's speech understand it easily.
A simple way to see it is that the formants are the same in every case, but a high voice gives the listener only a few harmonics to hear them through.

sections.title: Map spectra into a spectrogram

teaching.text: A **spectrogram** maps many spectra onto one display over time. **Time** runs along the horizontal axis, **frequency** runs up the vertical axis, and **darkness** shows how much energy, or amplitude, there is.

F0 can be measured in **Praat** by taking a little piece of speech, viewing a spectral slice and picking the lowest harmonic. One measured voice had F0 around 170 hertz, and the next harmonic sat at about twice that value.

sections.title: Reflection prompt

teaching.text: Saying **Where were you a year ago?** brings every idea about speech together in one short sentence. The vocal folds supply harmonics the whole time, and every new sound changes where the tongue and lips squeeze the air, so the formants keep moving from one moment to the next.
children: On a spectrogram of the sentence, **time** runs along the bottom, **frequency** runs up, and the **dark bands are the formants**.
Where the vowel sounds like **/i/**, **F2 rises high and F1 stays low**, because the squeeze lands where Mode 2 is springy and Mode 1 is massy.
During **you**, the formants **drop**, because rounding the lips adds mass right where the air moves the most, and that lowers all of them.
Through **a year ago**, F2 goes up and then down again as the tongue moves from one vowel to the next.

teaching.text: **All the formants are constantly changing during speech, so speech is not a string of frozen vowels.** Every rise and fall of a formant can be predicted with the same mass and spring reasoning, by asking where the constriction is and whether the air there is moving or compressing in each mode.
children: This constant change is why a network that sees two formants from one frozen moment cannot understand real speech, and why speech recognition needs systems that take in whole stretches of sound over time.
In plain terms, a spectrogram of a real sentence is a moving record of the tongue and lips, and reading it means following the dark bands as they rise and fall.

sections.title: Speech-complexity experiment prompt

teaching.text: A spliced recording reveals how complex speech perception is. The **m** part of a recorded **ma** is joined to the **a** part of a recorded **na**, and listeners clearly hear **na**, not ma.
children: **The perception of m or n comes more from the vowel than from the nasal sound itself.** After m, one formant of the vowel stays fairly **stationary**, and after n, that formant shows a **big drop**.

So listeners decide what consonant they heard **during the vowel**, after the consonant is over. This was one of the first striking results in speech perception, published in the **1950s** by the linguist **André Malécot**.

teaching.text: Listeners **take in whole stretches of speech and then decide** about the sounds that came first. For about seventy years, speech recognition machines that treated each slice as its own sound **failed**, and modern speech recognition relies on large language models that use what follows to decide about what came before.

sections.title: Use formants as input to vowel recognition

teaching.text: A **neural network** can be trained to recognize vowels from formants. Its **two inputs** are **F1 and F2**, measured from real recordings of five vowels, and its job is to decide which vowel was spoken.
children: **The knowledge of the network is in its weights**, which are learned from the data.

sections.title: A fully connected linear vowel network

teaching.text: The network has **five output neurons**, one for each word, **done, dune, dean, Don and Dan**, and **three hidden layers** with **3, 2 and 4 neurons**. Every neuron in one layer connects to every neuron in the next, so the network is **fully connected**.
children: This version is **purely linear**, meaning it has **no activation functions**, so each neuron just passes on the result of its inner product.

sections.title: Random weights assign signed contributions to connections

teaching.text: Before training, **every weight is a random number between minus one and one**. A **positive** weight makes its input push the next neuron up, and a **negative** weight makes its input push the next neuron down.
children: The example input is **F1 of 320 and F2 of 2000 hertz**, a very low F1 with a very high F2, which is the pattern of **/i/**, so the correct answer is **dean**.

sections.title: Forward flow and an illustrative output distribution

teaching.text: **Forward propagation** carries the input through the network one layer at a time, and each neuron computes an **inner product**, multiplying each incoming number by its weight and adding the results.

The output is a **probability distribution** over the five words, with values of **.5, .1, .1, .1 and .2**, which add up to one. With random weights the network puts its highest probability on **done**, so it is wrong.
children: The correct answer is given as the target distribution **0, 0, 1, 0, 0**, and **stochastic gradient descent** changes each weight so that next time the inner products lead to a high probability for dean.
In plain terms, the network starts out guessing, the target says what the right guess was, and learning nudges every weight so the right guess wins next time.

sections.title: Declare the layer sequence in PyTorch

teaching.text: **PyTorch** declares the network as a list of layers. **Sequential** means the network has **one layer after another, in a sequence**, and **Linear** means **do inner products** of weights and previous activations.
children: **nn.Linear(2, 3)** reads as **take input from 2 neurons, and have 3 neurons**. The next lines read 3 in and 2 out, then 2 in and 4 out, then 4 in and 5 out.
Turning off the **bias**, by setting it to False, keeps every layer purely linear, matching the diagram of the network.

teaching.text: **Only layers that do calculations get a line.** The **input layer** has no weights coming into it and does no inner products, so it never gets its own line, and the first line describes the **first hidden layer**.
children: This network has **five layers in total** but **three hidden layers**, and the **last line is always the output layer**, so the question has to be read carefully.

teaching.text: To **add a hidden layer of 3 neurons right before the output**, the old last line, 4 in and 5 out, becomes **4 in and 3 out**, and a new last line takes **3 in and gives 5 out**.
children: A quick check is that each line's first number must match the previous line's second number.

teaching.text: A network declared as 4 in and 3 out, 3 in and 8 out, 8 in and 4 out, 4 in and 4 out, and 4 in and 5 out takes **4 numbers as input**, has **four hidden layers** with 3, 8, 4 and 4 neurons, and decides among **5 categories**.
children: When the first category is correct, the target distribution puts a **1 in the first slot and 0 everywhere else**.

lecture15.title: Neural Networks · Forward propagation, learning, and sigmoid

sections.title: Neural Networks
Two formants feed a fully connected network

teaching.text: A **neural network** can act as a very simple **speech recognizer**. It takes the **two formants, F1 and F2**, of a vowel and decides which of **five words** it heard, **done, dune, dean, Don or Dan**. Networks like this are the **atoms** that modern **large language models** are built from.
The network has **2 input neurons**, **three hidden layers** with **3, 2 and 4 neurons**, and **5 output neurons**, and every neuron connects to every neuron in the next layer.
children: The **input neurons** just take numbers in from the environment, such as one speaker's F1 of 400 and F2 of 1900.

**The knowledge of the network is in its weights.** Each connection has a weight, a positive or negative number, and the whole network is nothing more than a machine for processing numbers with those weights.

sections.title: Forward propagation combines weighted inputs

teaching.text: **Forward propagation** carries one input through the network to a decision. The example input is **F1 of 320 and F2 of 2000**, which has the pattern of **dean**.
children: Each neuron computes an **inner product**. For the top neuron of the first hidden layer, the weight on F1 is multiplied by 320, the weight on F2 is multiplied by 2000, and the two products are added.
The result of that inner product, with no other change, is called the neuron's **linear activation**, and here it comes out slightly below zero.
The activations of each layer become the inputs to the next layer, which does more inner products, until the output layer.

teaching.text: At the end, the output numbers are turned into a **probability distribution**, numbers between zero and one that **add up to one** and stand for the network's **decision**. The operation that does this is called **softmax**, and all that matters about it is that a bigger number gives a bigger probability.
children: Here the network gives **done about 56 percent**, so it says, in effect, **"I heard done,"** even though the input was dean.

teaching.text: **Knowledge has been reduced to positive and negative numbers, and inference has been reduced to multiplying and adding.** The systems people chat with every day make their decisions with nothing but these elementary operations, which are close to what the chemistry inside real neurons does.

sections.title: Pop quiz · Forward propagation

teaching.text: Because every step is an inner product, the effect of raising one number can be worked out without any arithmetic. Take the top neuron of the last hidden layer, with an activation of about 1.57, and its weight of positive 0.1 into the **done** output.
children: If that **activation goes up**, its contribution to the done output goes up, so the **probability of done increases**.
If that **weight goes up**, from 0.1 to 0.2, the contribution also grows, so the **probability of done increases** again.
**A positive number times a positive number is positive**, so raising either one makes that neuron push the output up more.

teaching.text: A good answer names the direction, up or down, and then the reason, never the multiplication.
children: In plain terms, each neuron votes for each output through its weight, and a positive vote from an active neuron always helps that output.

sections.title: Info on Exam 2 and Exam 3
Backpropagation uses the difference between prediction and target

teaching.text: **Every network starts out stupid**, because its weights start out **random**, and it becomes smarter only by being told the right answer.
children: The **desired output** for a recording of dean is **0, 0, 1, 0, 0**, a 100 percent chance it was dean, which is called a **one-hot encoding**.
The gap between the **computed output** and the desired output is the network's **error**.

teaching.text: **Backpropagation** changes the weights so that the same input leads to a better decision. **Learning happens gradually, one step at a time**, just as with stochastic gradient descent, and the **learning rate** sets how big each step is.
children: The weights are updated **starting from the end**, first the weights into the output, then into the third hidden layer, then the second, then the first, while the forward activations stay as they were.
This is why AI needs huge **data centers**, since a modern chatbot can have **trillions of weights** that must be nudged over and over for months.

sections.title: Predict how changing a marked weight affects error

teaching.text: For the **last weight**, the 0.1 that links the top neuron of the last hidden layer to **done**, the effect is easy to see. Raising it would raise the probability of done, but the desired probability of done is **zero**, so raising it would make the error **worse**, and it should be **lowered**.

For the **first weight**, the 0.005 near the input, the effect is very hard to see. Changing it changes the first hidden layer, which changes the second and the third, which finally change the output.
children: **Its effect on the decision is mediated by all the intermediate calculations**, so just by looking at it, there is no way to tell whether it should go up or down. Backpropagation still works it out.

sections.title: Backpropagation reuses downstream error calculations

teaching.text: **The last weights directly determine the output probabilities**, so the error can be used right away to improve them. **The first weights affect their activations, which affect two more layers of activations**, and their effect on the error **includes the effect of the last weights**, which are downstream of them.

So **improving the last weights is the easy problem**, and improving the first weights is a much bigger problem that already contains the easy one. Solving small problems first so they can be used for bigger ones is **dynamic programming**, developed by **Bellman** and **Viterbi**.
children: **Backpropagation is stochastic gradient descent plus dynamic programming.** Stochastic gradient descent changes the numbers gradually, and dynamic programming supplies the **back** in backpropagation.
Backpropagation was worked out in the **mid-1980s**, and a 2024 Nobel Prize recognized it, because there would be no AI without it.

The short version of the exam answer is that the last weight affects the decision in one simple step, while the first weight's effect goes through many layers and depends on the later weights, so the easy problem is solved first and reused for the harder ones.

sections.title: Pair each recording with its target row

teaching.text: Training needs two tables of numbers, called **matrices**, and each row pairs **one recording** with **the vowel it really was**.
children: The **input matrix** has two columns, F1 and F2, so with about 110 recordings it is 110 by 2.
The **output matrix** has five columns, one for each word, with a **1 marking the true vowel**, so it is 110 by 5.

sections.title: Read one full-batch training step in PyTorch

teaching.text: A short **Python** program, using the **PyTorch** library, runs one training step.
children: The **import** lines bring in the torch library, which does all the background work, and the **load** lines read the formant matrix as X and the true-vowel matrix as Y.

**Sequential** means a **sequence of layers**, and each **Linear** line is a layer that **does inner products**. **nn.Linear(2, 3)** describes the first hidden layer, which takes 2 inputs and provides 3 outputs.
The network has **five layers** but only **four lines**, because the **input layer does no processing**.

teaching.text: The last lines carry out **one training step** using all 110 rows at once. **SGD** is stochastic gradient descent, **lr** is the **learning rate**, the **loss** measures the network's mistakes, **backward** runs backpropagation, and **step** changes the weights.
children: In plain terms, the program describes the network, shows it the data, measures how wrong it is, works backward to find who is to blame, and adjusts the weights a little.

sections.title: Sigmoid turns an inner product into a bounded activation

teaching.text: **Lord Edgar Adrian** won the **Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1932** for discovering that **neurons are nearly digital**, roughly **on or off**. The network's neurons so far are not like that, because their activations can be any real numbers.
The **sigmoid** is an **activation function** that takes the inner product and squashes it.
children: A **large negative** inner product, such as minus 4, minus 10 or minus 100, gives about **0**, so the neuron is **off**.
A **large positive** inner product, such as 4 or 100, gives about **1**, so the neuron is **on**.
Only inner products **near zero** get values in between, so the sigmoid **digitizes** the neuron.

teaching.text: The sigmoid also matches something about **perception**. **Some things that are very different are perceived as the same, and some things that are very similar are perceived as different.**
children: A friend is the same person with a hat or without one, just as the sigmoid gives minus 1000 and minus 20 the same value.
USC and UCLA are alike in many ways yet perceived as completely different, just as two inputs just below and just above zero land on opposite sides of the sigmoid's jump.
In plain terms, the flat parts of the curve lump different things together, and the steep middle splits nearly identical things apart.

sections.title: Apply sigmoid while recalculating downstream activity

teaching.text: Adding the sigmoid to each hidden neuron changes every number downstream. The first hidden neuron, slightly below zero, becomes about **0.4**, and the second, about 6.6, becomes about **1**, and each change recalculates the later layers.

With the same random weights and the sigmoid on all nine hidden neurons, the network spreads its probability more evenly and gives its highest probability to **Dan**, so it is **still wrong** about dean. Only training with backpropagation can give it good weights.

sections.title: Insert sigmoid after the hidden linear layers

teaching.text: The program changes in only one way. **nn.Sigmoid** is inserted after each **hidden** linear layer, which means "apply the sigmoid," or make that layer digital.
children: The **last layer has no sigmoid**, because its outputs go straight into the loss calculation, which turns them into probabilities.

teaching.text: Training both versions tests whether the sigmoid makes the vowel recognizer better or worse, and other functions such as **ReLU** can be swapped in too. **Many of the most basic ideas in AI come from how real brains work.**

lecture16.title: Neural Networks · Vowel data, training runs, and initialization

sections.title: Neural Networks
Two formants feed a fully connected network

teaching.text: This **neural network** simulates a very simple piece of human perception. It takes the **two formants**, F1 and F2, of an isolated vowel and decides which of five words it heard, with 2 input neurons, hidden layers of 3, 2 and 4 neurons, and 5 output neurons.

**The weights are the network's knowledge.** The network is told the right answer as a probability distribution, so for a speaker's /i/ it is told **0, 0, 1, 0, 0**. At first the weights are random, so the distribution it produces is very different, and the network learns by correcting that **mistake**.

sections.title: Forward propagation combines weighted inputs

teaching.text: **Forward propagation** carries the input through the network. With **F1 of 320 and F2 of 2000**, each neuron in the first hidden layer multiplies each formant by its weight and adds the results, and each later layer does the same with the activations before it.
children: With random weights, the network gives more than half of its probability to **done**, so it decides it heard done when the answer is dean.

teaching.text: To fix the mistake, **all the weights must change**, using **backpropagation**, which is made of **stochastic gradient descent** and **dynamic programming**.

sections.title: Pop quiz · Forward propagation

teaching.text: **Changing a weight at the very end is directly and immediately reflected in the output probabilities**, which are the network's decision.
children: The probability of done comes partly from a weight of 0.1 times an activation of about 1.57. Raising that weight would raise the probability of done, the opposite of what is wanted, so it should go **down**.

teaching.text: **Changing a weight near the input sets off a chain of changes** through every hidden layer before it reaches the decision, so deciding how to change it is a very hard problem.
children: That is why the weights at the end are the easier ones to change, and why backpropagation fixes them first.

sections.title: Vowel formants overlap across five categories

teaching.text: The real formant data from the class shows why AI is hard. Each recording is a dot, with **F1 along the horizontal axis** and **F2 up the vertical axis**, 525 dots in all, 105 for each vowel.
children: The data do show a pattern. The **/i/ dots sit high**, with a **high F2 and a low F1**, just as the theory predicts.
But there is **enormous overlap**. Many /æ/ dots sit among the /i/ dots, and the /u/, /a/ and schwa clouds pile on top of one another.

teaching.text: **If the vowels sat in separate clusters, AI would be easy.** Because they overlap, many points are ambiguous, and for a new speaker in the middle of the overlap the best answer is only the vowel whose dots are most common there.
children: Removing the differences between speakers, called **normalization**, was tried for about seventy years without success.
This overlap was first found in the early 1950s by **Peterson and Barney**, and good speech recognition only arrived around 2011 or 2012, with neural networks trained by backpropagation.

sections.title: Info on Exam 2 and Exam 3
Backpropagation uses the difference between prediction and target

teaching.text: **Stochastic gradient descent** is the same algorithm used to improve an average from data, now used to improve every weight, with the same **learning rate** and the same tradeoff between learning fast and learning accurately. **Dynamic programming** supplies the order, so the weights at the end are improved first and the hardest problem is solved last.
children: The error says which way each output should move. Done, at about 56 percent, should go down, dean should go up, and the others should go down.

sections.title: Predict how changing a marked weight affects error

teaching.text: For the last weights, it is easy to tell whether each should go up or down, because one inner product connects them to the decision. The network said done when the answer was dean, so any last weight that pushes done up should be **lowered**.

sections.title: Backpropagation reuses downstream error calculations

teaching.text: **Backpropagation changes the last weights first, then the ones before them, and so on to the first.** Each later problem is easier because something has already been learned from the problems solved before it.
children: Modern systems apply this to about **six trillion weights**, which is what the huge data centers are doing.
**Geoffrey Hinton** won the **2024 Nobel Prize in Physics** for backpropagation, which has roots in physics through dynamical systems.
In plain terms, the blame for a mistake is easiest to assign to the weights closest to the mistake, and that blame is then passed backward to the weights that came before.

sections.title: Pair each recording with its target row

teaching.text: Training uses **two matrices** of numbers, one with **F1 and F2** for each recording and one with the matching row of **zeros and a single one** for the true vowel. Learning picks a row, computes the decision, compares it with the true answer, and changes the weights if the decision is wrong.

**If the network makes the right decision, there is no error, so there is nothing to learn.** A network can keep getting the right answer by **memorizing** its data without learning the pattern underneath it.
children: Children learning English show the same thing, as **Carol Chomsky** observed. They first say **went** correctly from memory, then learn the regular pattern and say **goed**, and only later learn that went is an **exception**.
In plain terms, getting the right answer early can come from memory, and real learning sometimes shows up as new mistakes.

sections.title: Read one full-batch training step in PyTorch

teaching.text: **The import lines bring into Python the programs for doing inner products, backpropagation and related work**, so none of that has to be written by hand. This works because of **libraries**, an idea that goes back to **Margaret Hamilton's** software for **Apollo 11**, and around 2015 **Facebook** released **PyTorch** and **Google** released **TensorFlow**.

**Sequential means a network that is a sequence of layers**, and each **Linear** line is one processing layer that does inner products. **nn.Linear(2, 3)** says "I receive information from 2 neurons, and I have 3 neurons," and the input layer gets no line because it does no processing.

**SGD** is stochastic gradient descent, and **lr** is the **learning rate**, set here to 0.1. **A higher learning rate learns much faster but less accurately, and a lower learning rate learns more accurately but much more slowly.**
children: So changing the learning rate from 0.1 to 0.3 makes the network **learn faster**, but its **accuracy goes down**.
**Loss** is the **mistake**, **backward** is **backpropagation**, and **step** updates the weights.

sections.title: Sigmoid turns an inner product into a bounded activation

teaching.text: **Lord Edgar Adrian** discovered in the 1920s that **neurons are nearly digital**, either **firing** or **not firing**. The **sigmoid** works like this discovery, taking an inner product and giving back a number between zero and one.
children: An inner product of **minus 4**, minus 6 or minus 1000 gives about **zero**, so the neuron is **off**, and one of **4**, 6 or 100 gives about **one**, so the neuron is **on**.
So the sigmoid **digitizes** neural processing, the way brain chemistry does.

teaching.text: **Some things that seem alike are perceived as different, and some things that are very different are perceived as the same**, and the sigmoid captures both.

sections.title: Apply sigmoid while recalculating downstream activity

teaching.text: Applying the sigmoid one hidden neuron at a time changes the whole calculation downstream, because every later activation is recalculated. With the sigmoid on all nine hidden neurons and the same random weights, the network's choice moves from done to Dan, so it is still wrong until it is trained.

sections.title: Insert sigmoid after the hidden linear layers

teaching.text: In the program, **nn.Sigmoid** is added after each hidden linear layer, and the last layer gets no sigmoid because its outputs go into the loss calculation. The sigmoid can also be replaced by functions such as **ReLU** to test whether recognition improves.
children: **AI is duplicating abilities that animals have.** Its most fundamental ideas come from discoveries about how brains work, with computer scientists adding ideas of their own on top.

sections.title: One initialization · training the linear network for 2,000 updates

teaching.text: The full training program runs **2000 updates** with a learning rate of 0.1 and records the **accuracy**, the percent of recordings classified correctly, after every update.
**The accuracy starts at 20 percent.** With random weights the network knows nothing, but with **five vowels**, even a random guess is right **one time out of five**, which is called **chance**.
children: With **ten categories**, chance would be **10 percent**.

teaching.text: After a while the accuracy **jumps up to about 40 percent**, so the network is learning something, and then it **levels off** near **45 percent**. Each pass of learning is called an **epoch**.

sections.title: Ten initializations · different paths, the same final accuracy

teaching.text: Training was repeated **ten times**, each time from a **different set of random weights**, called a **seed**. The runs take **different paths**, one staying at chance for about 500 epochs and another jumping up early, but **all ten end at the same accuracy**, close to 45 percent.
children: Children learning language are similar. Homes that talk mostly about sports or mostly about politics give children different words, yet by about age four they speak the same language.

teaching.text: **The network levels off near 40 percent, not 100, because the data overlap so much.** For a point in the middle of the overlap, even a person would have to guess, and AI is not magic.
children: Adding or removing layers, or changing the number of neurons, tests whether the 40 percent can be improved.

sections.title: NNs → LLMs → Agentic Systems
Neural networks, 1943–1986 · a static vector and a few categories

teaching.text: A **neural network** takes in information about one moment, uses its **weights** to process it and makes a decision, and it learns those weights through **backpropagation**. The idea began in **1943** with a paper by **McCulloch and Pitts**, which starts from the **all-or-none** character of nervous activity, the same idea as the **sigmoid**.
children: Warren McCulloch was a **psychiatrist**, and the earliest work on neural networks aimed to model how the mind works, not to make money.

teaching.text: By **1986**, the two **Parallel Distributed Processing** books had matured these ideas. **Parallel** means many neurons compute at the same time, and **distributed** means the information is spread across all the neurons, and one contributor, **Geoffrey Hinton**, later won the **2024 Nobel Prize in Physics**.
**Given some static vector of formants, these networks could make a decision about a few possible categories**, but **human cognition is far more complex**.
children: **Speech is incredibly time-varying**, because every moment gives a new set of formants, and **language is time-varying too**, since a sentence is many words in a row.
So giving a network one list of numbers can never model cognition that unfolds in time.

sections.title: Jordan’s recurrent network for speech production

teaching.text: In **1985**, **Michael Jordan** developed **recurrent neural networks** to make sense of **speech production**, meaning how the tongue, the velum and the lips move over time. Features such as nasality, backness and lip rounding each switch on and off at different moments, and a regular network could never handle something that complex and time-varying.
children: His network is **not just sequential**, because it has **two layers working in parallel**.
It is called **recurrent** because it **takes its output and sends it back into part of its input**, using what it produced at one moment to predict the next.

teaching.text: **GPT works the same way, one word at a time.** It predicts the next word, feeds the prompt plus that word back in, and predicts the next word again, so the idea behind GPT starts with thinking about how speech unfolds in time.
children: People refined the recurrent network until **2017**, when the **large language model** was invented. These years give a sense of the history, but they will not be asked about.

sections.title: From one neuron to agentic systems

teaching.text: AI systems build up in steps, and **each step is made of the one before it**.
children: **A single neuron takes in a vector and gives back one number** through an **inner product**, multiplying each input by its weight and adding them up.
**A neural network takes in one vector and gives back a whole decision vector**, through many inner products.

teaching.text: **A large language model takes in many vectors, one for each moment in a sequence, and gives back one decision vector about what comes next.** Picture 15 vectors, each standing for one word, and the job is to **predict the sixteenth**.
children: In real systems, the **context window** holds hundreds of thousands to a million vectors, each thousands of numbers long.
The sixteenth vector is a **probability distribution over the next word**, with one entry for each of about 30,000 English words.

teaching.text: **An LLM is a dynamical system**, which is why the Nobel Prize for AI was awarded in physics. Its input vectors are its **initial condition**, and each layer turns them into **better vectors**, until the last layer can predict the next word.
children: In plain terms, an LLM is like the oscillator, except that thousands of numbers are refined layer by layer instead of two numbers changing over time.

teaching.text: **An agentic system is a graph of LLMs**, such as an outline LLM, a writing LLM, a **critic LLM**, a revision LLM and a final LLM. The critic is what greatly reduced **hallucination**, and the back-and-forth is why many systems take a while to respond.

**The chief insight behind all of this is Gestalt completion.** People see a triangle in the Gestalt figure even though none is drawn, and training a system only to **predict the missing thing** turns out to emulate human cognition.
children: The same idea is behind the **cloze procedure**, a test introduced by **Wilson Taylor** in **1953**, in which words are deleted from a text and people fill them in. The name comes from **closure**, the Gestalt term for completing a familiar pattern that is not quite finished, such as seeing a broken circle as whole.
**Knowledge can be tested by asking someone to complete a sequence, and for AI, completion is all that knowledge is.** An LLM predicting the next word is playing a cloze game over and over.
Underneath everything, **inference is inner products**, and **learning is stochastic gradient descent plus dynamic programming**.

sections.title: Fifteen vectors · the same next-item question for any sequence

teaching.text: **An LLM takes 15 vectors and predicts the sixteenth**, and the vectors can stand for almost anything.
children: They can be **words**, as in "The cat that the dog chased ran up the old tree and sat on the," where getting the next word right means knowing it was the cat that sat.
They can be **slices of sound** from a spectrogram, which in 2019 gave the **best speech recognition in 75 years** and now powers synthetic voices that are hard to tell from humans.
They can be **patches of an image**, which became the basis of modern **computer vision**.
They can be **amino acids** in a protein, and that work on **protein folding** won the **2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry**.

teaching.text: **The LLM only ever sees vectors**, so one design asks one question every time, what comes sixteenth. Because it predicts from past data, something the past data does not cover can make it **hallucinate**.

sections.title: Which sequences can be English words?

teaching.text: English allows only **certain sequences of sounds** in its words. **A simple English syllable can have a consonant, then a vowel, then a consonant**, as in Don, mat, sit, cup, dog and fish, and the pattern is about **sounds, not letters**.
Syllables can also have **clusters**. A cluster before the vowel is an **onset**, as in split, flat and black, and one after the vowel is a **coda**, as in desk, help and lamp.
children: Each real word has an impossible twin, such as **flat** and **lfat**, **help** and **hepl**, and **lamp** and **lapm**, so order matters.
**The order mirrors around the vowel.** The l sits right next to the vowel in both flat and help, and each impossible twin puts the wrong consonant against the vowel.

teaching.text: **A long word is a chain of syllables.** The sounds t and l are fine across a syllable break, as in Atlantic, but **tl cannot start a syllable**, and **ng** can end a syllable, as in ring, but never start one.

sections.title: Guessing the next letter reveals phonotactic knowledge

teaching.text: **Guessing the next letter of an English word reveals this sound knowledge.** After a vowel, as in "ra," almost anything can follow, but at the start of a word the choices narrow sharply.
children: After **sp**, the next letter is l, r or a vowel, and never n, and after **k** it is a vowel or n, as in knee.
After **skr**, or after **m** at the start of a word, only a vowel can come.
After **bram**, the letter b is almost forced, as in bramble.

teaching.text: **Guessing the next letter is predicting the sixteenth item**, the same game an LLM plays. Its prediction is a **probability distribution** that is **flat** after "ra" and **sharply peaked** after "skr," because English allows nothing else there.
children: In plain terms, the more the letters so far restrict what can come next, the more the probability piles onto a few letters.

sections.title: Build an LLM together

teaching.text: English syllables are a good test case, because English has only about 26 letters or a few dozen sounds, so a small LLM can learn the syllable knowledge every speaker has. The plan is to **design an agentic system using instructions written in English**, which builds the LLM, trains it to predict each next letter, and shows what it has learned along the way.

lecture18.title: Neuron, Neural Networks, LLMs and Agents

sections.title: Neuron, neural networks, LLMs and agents
From a neuron to agents that communicate

teaching.text: Everything in modern AI grows from **one very simple idea**, the **neuron**, which takes information from other neurons through an **inner product**. A **neural network** repeats that operation layer after layer to make a decision, but a network that makes one **static decision** cannot capture cognition that **unfolds in time**.

**Language depends on long-distance relationships between words.** In "the dog that my parents, who I love very much, who live in a state far, far away," the next word is **barks**, because it goes with the singular **dog** no matter how many words come in between.
children: Speakers absorb this rule without being taught, and an LLM learns it the same way, from data, which is why it needs so many layers.

teaching.text: **An agentic system is a team of LLMs that talk to each other in English.** An outline LLM plans, a writing LLM writes, a critic LLM checks, and a revision LLM loops with the critic, sometimes under a **controller** agent.
children: The agents are also **multilingual in computer languages**, such as Python and database languages, because they were trained to predict whole programs too.
Agents share a **common memory**, which is a big source of their power and also of the danger, because it lets them coordinate in ways nobody planned.

teaching.text: **Nobody fully understands what all the weights are doing**, because the designs evolved by tinkering over about 75 years, much as dogs were bred into today's breeds.

sections.title: Parallel heads and successive layers

teaching.text: **Predicting the next word is so difficult that an LLM needs many layers, and in each layer it needs many parallel heads.** A head is a separate expert, and in each layer the knowledge from all the heads is brought together to produce **improved vectors**.
children: This is a question for the exam. **Layers go one after another from the input to the output, and heads sit side by side within each layer.**

teaching.text: **A classroom comparison makes heads and layers clear.** Imagine trying to improve oneself by visiting a series of classes, one after another.
children: In each class, every student gives an independent opinion, and each student is like a **head**.
The opinions are **combined** into one improved version, which is what a layer does with its heads, and then the next class is visited. **The classes are the layers.**
In plain terms, layers give an LLM its depth, one round of improvement after another, and heads give it width, many experts consulted at once within each round.

teaching.text: **Each head is a set of weights**, and large systems have **a hundred or more layers** with on the order of **a hundred heads** in each. When the system predicts the wrong word, **every head in every layer** adjusts its weights through backpropagation.

sections.title: A dynamical rule across time and depth

teaching.text: **A dynamical system is a rule that is fed back to itself.** Numbers go in, the rule acts on them, and the output is fed back in as the next input, again and again.
children: In the **harmonic oscillator**, x and v **take turns**, the new x computed from the old v and the new v from the new x, and step by step the rule draws a **cosine**.
Fields as far apart as finance use the same idea with different rules.

teaching.text: **Jordan's network was a marriage of neural networks and dynamical systems.** Its **output is copied back into its state units**, and **plan units** and **state units** feed the hidden layer, with the same weights used at every step. After more than **thirty years of tinkering**, this idea became the **LLM**.

**In an LLM, the layer is the rule**, and **depth plays the role of time**. Each layer applies its weights to every vector, and following one number up through the layers traces out a curve, much like the oscillator's curve, though not an exact cosine.
children: The rule in each layer is the weights of its heads, learned through backpropagation by predicting the next word.
The goal is to understand this general structure, not to memorize formulas.

sections.title: One prediction task for different sequences

teaching.text: An LLM is given **15 vectors** and asked to predict the **16th**, and the vectors can come from anywhere, because the machine only ever sees lists of numbers.
children: They can be **15 words** of a sentence, **15 frames of a spectrogram**, **15 patches of an image** read row by row, or **15 amino acids** in a protein, such as the B chain of insulin.

teaching.text: **The same design and the same prediction game work for language, speech, vision and proteins.**

sections.title: Which sequences can be English words?

teaching.text: Speakers know a small system of **only a few dozen sounds** that decides how vowels and consonants can follow each other, which makes it a good test case for a small LLM. **A simple English syllable is a consonant, then a vowel, then a consonant**, and only certain **clusters** are allowed, so **sblit**, **lfat** and **desb** are impossible.

**Every language has its own rules for sequences.** Mandarin allows only nasal sounds at the end of a syllable, Cantonese also allows a final p, Russian and Polish allow clusters like zb or dl at the start of a word, and Spanish speakers add an e before a word like stadium.

sections.title: Guessing the next letter reveals phonotactic knowledge

teaching.text: Guessing the next letter of an English word reveals this sound knowledge directly. **After a vowel, almost anything can follow**, but **at the start of a word the choices narrow sharply**, so after **sp** only l, r or a vowel can come, and after **skr** only a vowel.

**Guessing the next letter is predicting the 16th vector.** A GPT that only plays this game learns English sounds and spelling, with a **flat** distribution after a vowel and a **sharply peaked** one after skr.

sections.title: Design an agentic system for English syllables

teaching.text: An LLM that learns English syllables can be built by **describing it in English** to an agentic system, specifying **five layers**, **four heads in each layer**, and **input vectors 64 numbers long**, then training it on **1000 English words** to **predict the next letter** and showing ten generated words after each step.
children: The system built a small **character-level transformer** with **attention heads**, where **attention** means a head consults the rest of the sequence to work out which preceding items matter, just as predicting barks requires attending to dog.
After training, the generated words were **still mostly gibberish**, and training on **10,000 words** for many more steps was the suggested next change.

teaching.text: **Software 1.0** is writing programs, **Software 2.0** is letting a network's **weights** become the program, and **Software 3.0** is using an agentic system to build and run a program from plain English, which is called **vibe coding**.

The first attempt at this kind of problem was **Claude Shannon's 1948 paper, "A Mathematical Theory of Communication,"** which generated letter sequences closer and closer to English by hand and founded **information theory**, which remains important for LLMs today.
